    7. Integrity and Reconciliation (edits by other tools)

    On open, Reviera checks: 1. Manifest. DataId is present. The hash of each document matches its Sha256. If a document is corrupt, it is opened read-only, reported, and can be restored from backup. 2. Element data. For each element with Reviera_Element, Reviera recomputes the hash of its current IFC representation and compares it with GeomHash: - Equal: the recipe is authoritative and the element stays fully parametric. - Different: the element was edited outside Reviera, and its recipe is marked stale. On the first edit, the user chooses between keep external geometry (the recipe is dropped and the element becomes a non-parametric IFC element) and regenerate from recipe. 3. Dangling references. For RXD references to GlobalIds that no longer exist: - annotation attached to them (tags, dimension references) is removed and listed - constraints that use them are removed - view element overrides that use them are removed 4. Elements without data. New elements with no Reviera_Element (created by other tools) are imported as non-parametric elements: selectable, editable as IFC geometry, schedulable. 5. Report. A reconciliation report appears in the Warnings dialog and is stored as project/reconcile_log.

    8. BIMserver Mode

    • Model data. Embedded RXD travels as ordinary IFC objects in each check-in and download. No special transport is needed, and BIMserver's object-level storage, queries and merging keep it, because it is ordinary property sets. Each element's data stays attached to its element.
    • Merging (sync).
    • IFC objects are merged by GlobalId.
    • RXD objects are merged by id in a three-way merge against the common base revision. Fields changed on only one side merge automatically; the same field changed on both sides is a conflict for the user to resolve; a delete on one side against an edit on the other is also a conflict.
    • Element-level RXD follows its element's merge result.
    • Live ownership and locks (the worksharing "borrowing" equivalent). These change constantly and must not need new revisions, so they use BIMserver Extended Data on the latest revision. The calls below are confirmed in the public BIMserver ServiceInterface source: 1. Register schema org.reviera.ownership/1.0 (addExtendedDataSchema; look it up with getExtendedDataSchemaByName). 2. Publish: uploadFile, then addExtendedDataToRevision(roid, …). 3. Read: getLastExtendedDataOfRevisionAndSchema(roid, schemaId), then getFile. 4. Refresh on notification, or poll every 30 seconds; concurrency is optimistic. 5. Locks are advisory, matching what BIMserver supports. Reviera ships no enforcement plugin (TECH_STACK §5, decision 8).
    • External carrier with BIMserver. If a project uses the external carrier, the .reviera file is attached to each revision as Extended Data (schema org.reviera.rxd/1.0).

    9. Saving, Security, Performance, Versioning

    • Atomic save.
    • Embedded mode: write to a temporary file, fsync it, then rename it over the original.
    • External mode: write both files to temporaries, then rename the IFC first and the sidecar second.
    • Rotating backups keep IFC and sidecar paired.
    • Security.
    • RXD must not contain executable content. The one exception is project Lua macros, stored in document scripts/<name>. Macros are disabled until the user trusts them, and then run at the chosen Lua sandbox level.
    • Decoders enforce limits on decompressed size and chunk count.
    • The external ZIP carrier rejects path traversal.
    • Performance.
    • RXD documents are decoded in parallel (rayon).
    • View annotation is loaded lazily, when its view is first opened. With the embedded carrier this still works: the IFC parser reads the Reviera_Doc:views/annotation/<viewId> property sets as raw strings, and decompression, JSON parsing and object construction are deferred until the view is opened. (This answers Chapter 5 question Q5-7.)
    • Large numeric arrays may use zstd+base64 binary buffers, described in the style of glTF: { "buffer": "<doc>#bin0", "type": "f64", "count": n }.
    • Versioning. FormatVersion uses MAJOR.MINOR.
    • Minor versions only add things. Unknown kinds, fields and extension namespaces are kept as-is on save.
    • A major version change triggers a migration on open, and Reviera warns before saving a file that older versions can't read.
    • Add-in data. Add-ins store their data under reverse-DNS namespaces in ext (for example "org.example.acoustics"), or in documents named addins/<namespace>/…, and must register a JSON Schema for it.

    10. Compatibility Test Suite (required)

    Test Pass condition
    Schema validity Every saved file passes the IfcOpenShell validator and the buildingSMART validation service: schema and normative rules
    Round-trip: IfcOpenShell (Bonsai) Open, edit an unrelated element, save; RXD Psets are intact and GeomHash is unchanged for the untouched elements
    Round-trip: Open Source BIMserver Check in, then download; every Reviera_* Pset is byte-identical after decoding
    Round-trip: other IFC tools (a list kept in the test plan) Record whether Reviera_* Psets are kept. Tools that strip them are documented with "use external carrier" guidance
    Viewer behaviour Common IFC viewers open embedded-RXD files without errors or warnings
    Clean export strip_rxd output contains no Reviera_* names and gives an identical building model
    Reconciliation A wall's geometry edited in a third-party tool is detected as stale; a deleted wall removes its tags and dimensions, with a report

    11. Requirements

    ID Requirement Priority
    DM-RXD-001 Reviera shall store non-IFC data only as RXD documents and element data, using the schemas defined in this chapter. Read access for scripts and agents is rxd.get_document(path) -> JSON, which returns one decoded document by its canonical path (§6.4), and rxd.get_element_data(element) -> JSON, which returns the Reviera_Element or Reviera_Type payload of the element with that GlobalId. Both fail with rxd.not_found when the document or data is absent; neither can write. P0
    DM-RXD-002 By default, Reviera shall embed RXD in the IFC file using only Reviera_* property sets with IfcText and IfcLabel values, as in §3; the file shall remain schema-valid. file.save(document_id?) -> status writes the active (or named) document in its current carrier, atomically (§9). P0
    DM-RXD-003 Payload encoding shall follow §3.3: ASCII-only JSON or zstd+base64, chunks of at most 32,000 characters, canonical JSON, and a hash on each document. rxd.validate() -> report checks every document of the active project against its JSON Schema, its chunk sequence and its Sha256, and lists failures by document path without changing anything. P0
    DM-RXD-004 Reviera shall support the external carrier (.reviera file or folder, .rvb bundle) holding identical documents, chosen per project. The carrier is chosen with file.save_as(document_id?, path, kind?, format?, carrier?) -> status, where carrier is embedded, external_file, external_dir or bundle. When the lookup on open (§5) finds no sidecar, file.locate_rxd(path) -> status binds a .reviera file or folder chosen by the user; a sidecar whose DataId does not match the manifest is refused. P1
    DM-RXD-005 Reviera shall provide Export clean IFC and Export IFC with documentation. P0 / P1
    DM-RXD-006 Reviera shall detect external edits (GeomHash), dangling references and missing data, and reconcile them with a report (§7). rxd.reconcile(mode: report\|apply, drop_orphans?=true) -> report runs the checks on demand: report only lists findings, apply performs the removals as one undoable transaction and appends to project/reconcile_log. P0
    DM-RXD-007 Unknown RXD kinds, fields and extension namespaces shall survive a round trip unchanged. P0
    DM-RXD-008 In BIMserver mode, RXD shall travel inside the IFC; ownership state shall use Extended Data (§8); sync shall perform the three-way RXD merge. P1
    DM-RXD-009 Project macros stored in RXD shall be disabled until trusted. rxd.trust_scripts(scope: once\|always, sandbox level) -> status records the user's decision for the current document GUID and script hashes; always is remembered until a script changes, and the level can never exceed the user's maximum in Script Security (Ch 2 §2.13.7). P0
    DM-RXD-010 The compatibility test suite (§10) shall run in CI on every release. P0
    DM-RXD-011 The RXD JSON Schemas shall be published under the MIT licence (owner decision, 2026-10-12), separately from the GPL-3.0-or-later application, so that any tool, including proprietary ones, can read and write RXD. The format definition (this chapter) is published with them as the RXD package. See §12. P1

    Acceptance criteria - [ ] A Reviera project saved by default is a single .ifc file that passes schema validation and reopens in Reviera with all views, sheets and parametric intent restored. - [ ] The same file opens in a third-party IFC viewer without errors, showing the complete building. - [ ] Re-saving an unchanged project produces identical RXD payload bytes (deterministic output). - [ ] A document of 10 MB is chunked, and reassembles to the same Sha256. - [ ] A project switched to the external carrier and back is identical in content.

    12. Licensing of the RXD Schemas

    • Licence. The RXD JSON Schemas are licensed under the MIT licence (SPDX MIT). The rest of Reviera remains GPL-3.0-or-later.
    • Repository layout.
    • The schemas live in a self-contained directory, schemas/rxd/, with its own LICENSE file (MIT text, Copyright (c) <year> Reviera contributors) and a README.md stating the scope of the licence.
    • Each schema file carries "$comment": "SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT".
    • The schemas are also released as a separate versioned package (for example reviera-rxd-schemas-1.0.zip, plus an npm/crates package if useful).
    • Scope of the MIT grant. It covers the JSON Schema files, the example documents and the format description that ships with them (this chapter, exported as the package README/SPEC.md).
    • Not covered: Reviera's Rust code that reads and writes RXD. That code stays GPL-3.0-or-later. Rust types generated from the schemas inside the Reviera repository are part of the GPL application.
    • Third parties may generate their own code from the MIT schemas under any licence.
    • Contributions. Changes to schemas/rxd/ are accepted under MIT. The CI licence check enforces SPDX MIT for that path and GPL-3.0-or-later everywhere else.
    • Compatibility. MIT-licensed files inside a GPL-3.0-or-later project are fully compatible: the combined application is distributed under the GPL, and the schema files keep their MIT terms when distributed on their own.
    • Schema identifiers. $id URIs use https://nodeskreviera.org/schemas/rxd/<major>.<minor>/<name>.schema.json (owner, 2026-10-12, DM-RXD-OD2; one-word domains were taken). The domain is provisional until the project registers it, which must happen before 1.0 ships, and the URLs must then resolve to the published MIT schemas. Once a schema version is released its $id never changes, so the domain is effectively permanent from 1.0 on.

    13. Commands

    Command Parameters Returns Undoable Req ID
    file.save document_id? (default: active) status No DM-RXD-002
    file.save_as document_id? (default: active), path, kind?, format?: ifc|ifczip, carrier?: embedded|external_file|external_dir|bundle status No DM-RXD-004
    export.ifc (options defined here; base command in Ch 2 DM-FILE-004) path, setup? (name, id or inline settings), settings_override?, schema?, strip_rxd?=false, documentation?, background? job_id (the job result carries the export report) No DM-RXD-005
    file.locate_rxd path to an external .reviera file or folder status No DM-RXD-004
    rxd.validate — report No DM-RXD-003
    rxd.reconcile mode: report|apply, drop_orphans?=true report Yes DM-RXD-006
    rxd.get_document path JSON No (read) DM-RXD-001
    rxd.get_element_data element (GlobalId) JSON No (read) DM-RXD-001
    rxd.trust_scripts scope: once/always, sandbox level status No DM-RXD-009

    These are also exposed read-only as the MCP resources reviera://rxd/{path} and reviera://element/{guid}/rxd. Writes always go through domain commands, never through raw document editing.

    2bCHChapter 2b: Live Model Store and Crash Recovery

    ID prefix: DM-LIVE · Status: Draft 0.2 · 2026-10-12 (open questions OD1–OD5 accepted by the owner: sketch-session recovery, encryption at rest, time travel, unified BIMserver timeline, shared snapshots) Origin: Project-owner feature directive (2026-10-12): "Maintain the model live on disk as a SQLite database; on application crash, work can be restored from a near real-time on-disk representation." This is a Reviera-originated feature. It has no counterpart in the functional reference, which offers only interval-based autosave reminders and backups.

    Related: Chapter 2 §2.6–2.7 (regeneration, transactions, undo), Chapter 2a (RXD), Chapter 6 (BIMserver working copies), TECH_STACK.md §3.3.

    1. Concept

    Layer Role Durability
    In-memory model (Rust element DB, IfcOpenShell instance graph, RXD objects) Where editing and regeneration happen Volatile
    Live store: *.rvlive, a SQLite database in WAL mode A near real-time mirror of the model, updated after every committed transaction Survives crashes, power loss bounded by synchronous mode (§5)
    Project file: .ifc with embedded RXD (Chapter 2a) Canonical, interoperable deliverable, written on Save Durable and portable

    The live store does not replace IFC as the file format. Compatibility remains the first priority. The live store is a local, private working representation, comparable to a database's write-ahead log combined with a materialised state. When work is saved normally the live store is simply in step. When Reviera exits abnormally, it is the source of recovery.

     command ──► Transaction Manager ──commit──► in-memory model (regeneration done)
                                   │
                                   └─► ChangeSet (forward + inverse, dirty entities, RXD deltas)
                                            │  bounded channel (non-blocking for UI)
                                            ▼
                                   Live-store writer thread ──► SQLite (WAL)
                                            │   group commit ≤ 250 ms
                                            ▼
                                     *.rvlive  ──(on Save)──► project.ifc (atomic write)

    2. File Location and Ownership

    Item Rule
    Default location The per-user data directory: <data_dir>/Reviera/live/<project-key>.rvlive. On Linux <data_dir> is ~/.local/share; on Windows it is %LOCALAPPDATA%; on macOS it is ~/Library/Application Support. <project-key> is a hash of the project's canonical path plus the Reviera_Manifest.DataId.
    Why not beside the project file? SQLite locking is unreliable on network file systems (SMB/NFS), and projects often live on shared drives. Keeping the live store on local disk avoids corruption and keeps an unsaved working state out of shared folders.
    Optional location A preference may place the store beside the project as .<name>.rvlive. Reviera warns if that path is on a network file system.
    Companion files SQLite's -wal and -shm files, plus <key>.lock, which holds the PID, hostname, start time and a heartbeat timestamp.
    Single writer A live store is opened by exactly one Reviera process. A second instance opening the same project is offered read-only mode or Open a copy. A lock is stale when its PID no longer exists, or its heartbeat is older than 30 s and the host matches.
    New/untitled projects Get a live store immediately, keyed by a session UUID. Crash recovery therefore also covers work that was never saved.

    Commands. live.status() -> {path, head_seq, saved_seq, pending, last_commit_at, size} reports where the active project's store is, how far it has been written and how many change sets are still queued; the status-bar recovery indicator reads the same values (DM-LIVE-001).

    3. Database Schema (version 1)

    All tables are STRICT, the encoding is UTF-8, and SQLite must be 3.37 or later.

    -- identity and state of this live store
CREATE TABLE meta (
  key   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  value TEXT NOT NULL
) STRICT;
-- keys: schema_version, app_version, project_path, ifc_schema, data_id,
--       base_ifc_sha256 (IFC the session was opened from), saved_seq (last txn persisted to IFC),
--       head_seq (last txn applied here), clean_shutdown ('0'/'1'), session_id, opened_at, mode ('local'|'bimserver')

-- materialised IFC instance graph (everything except Reviera_* carrier Psets, see §3.1)
CREATE TABLE ifc_entity (
  sid        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         -- stable store id (= IfcOpenShell instance id at load; new ids allocated monotonically)
  ifc_type   TEXT    NOT NULL,            -- e.g. IFCWALL
  global_id  TEXT,                        -- rooted entities only
  step       TEXT    NOT NULL,            -- canonical STEP attribute list, e.g. ('2O2Fr$t4X7Zf8NOew3FLOH',#5,'Wall-001',$,...)
  seq        INTEGER NOT NULL             -- txn that last wrote this row
) STRICT;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ifc_entity_gid ON ifc_entity(global_id) WHERE global_id IS NOT NULL;
CREATE INDEX ifc_entity_type ON ifc_entity(ifc_type);

-- decoded RXD (Chapter 2a): project documents and element/type data, stored as JSON for direct access
CREATE TABLE rxd_document (
  path  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,                 -- canonical path, e.g. views/0192a3f5-...
  kind  TEXT NOT NULL,
  json  TEXT NOT NULL,                    -- canonical JSON
  seq   INTEGER NOT NULL
) STRICT;
CREATE TABLE rxd_element (
  global_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,             -- element or type GlobalId
  scope     TEXT NOT NULL,                -- 'element' | 'type'
  json      TEXT NOT NULL,
  geom_hash TEXT,
  seq       INTEGER NOT NULL
) STRICT;

-- transaction journal: every committed transaction, in order
CREATE TABLE txn (
  seq        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         -- monotonically increasing
  at         TEXT    NOT NULL,            -- ISO-8601 UTC
  origin     TEXT    NOT NULL,            -- ui | lua | addin:<ns> | mcp:<client> | sync | system
  name       TEXT    NOT NULL,            -- user-visible undo label, e.g. "Create Wall"
  command    TEXT,                        -- registry command name(s), JSON array
  params     TEXT,                        -- JSON (credentials never stored)
  group_id   INTEGER,                     -- transaction group (one undo step)
  forward    BLOB    NOT NULL,            -- zstd(changeset: entity/RXD upserts+deletes)
  inverse    BLOB    NOT NULL,            -- zstd(inverse changeset) — undo after recovery
  undone     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0   -- 1 if currently undone (redo stack)
) STRICT;

-- optional derived caches (rebuildable; may be dropped at any time)
CREATE TABLE cache_tessellation (
  global_id TEXT, lod TEXT, geom_hash TEXT, mesh BLOB,
  PRIMARY KEY (global_id, lod)
) STRICT;

-- interactive tool / sketch sessions in progress (§6.5): journaled micro-operations, not yet model transactions
CREATE TABLE session (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  kind       TEXT NOT NULL,               -- sketch | tool | family_editor | group_edit | in_place
  owner      TEXT,                        -- element GlobalId being edited, or new-element placeholder
  tool       TEXT NOT NULL,               -- registry tool id, e.g. floor.create
  context    TEXT NOT NULL,               -- JSON: active view, work plane, type, options, selection
  started_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  state      TEXT NOT NULL                -- open | committed | cancelled
) STRICT;
CREATE TABLE session_op (
  session_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES session(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  n          INTEGER NOT NULL,            -- order within session
  at         TEXT NOT NULL,
  op         TEXT NOT NULL,               -- JSON micro-op: add_curve, move_vertex, delete_curve, set_option, pick_point, ...
  PRIMARY KEY (session_id, n)
) STRICT;

-- time-travel keyframes (§8.5): compressed full-state snapshots bounding reconstruction cost
CREATE TABLE snapshot (
  seq        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,         -- state after this txn
  at         TEXT NOT NULL,
  reason     TEXT NOT NULL,               -- save | interval | session_start | manual
  label      TEXT,                        -- user-named snapshot (optional)
  data       BLOB NOT NULL                -- zstd(canonical dump of ifc_entity + rxd_* at seq)
) STRICT;

-- BIMserver mode: base revision for three-way merge (Chapter 6)
CREATE TABLE base_entity (
  sid INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ifc_type TEXT NOT NULL, global_id TEXT, step TEXT NOT NULL
) STRICT;
CREATE TABLE base_rxd (
  key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, json TEXT NOT NULL
) STRICT;

    3.1 What is stored

    Stored Not stored
    IFC entities, as canonical STEP attribute text per instance. This is lossless: it is exactly what IfcOpenShell would write. RXD carrier Psets (Reviera_*). RXD lives decoded in rxd_* and is re-encoded only when writing IFC.
    RXD objects, as canonical JSON Regenerated B-rep geometry. It can be derived from IFC plus RXD; at most an optional tessellation cache is kept.
    The committed transaction journal, with forward and inverse change sets —
    Interactive sessions in progress (sketches, multi-click tools, family-editor and group-edit sessions), as journaled micro-operations (§6.5) —
    Time-travel keyframe snapshots (§8.5) —
    Session metadata Credentials, API tokens and MCP session secrets

    4. Write Path

    1. Commit. When a model transaction commits (Chapter 2 §2.7), the Transaction Manager emits a ChangeSet. It contains: - the upserted and deleted IFC instances (by sid), as STEP text - the RXD documents and element data that changed - the forward and inverse deltas
    2. Enqueue. The ChangeSet goes onto a bounded channel to the live-store writer thread. The UI thread never waits on disk I/O. - If the channel is full, after 64 pending change sets or 64 MB, the next commit applies back-pressure, briefly blocking the issuer. The status bar shows "Writing recovery data…".
    3. Group commit. The writer batches change sets that arrive within 250 ms (configurable from 50 to 2,000 ms) into one SQLite transaction. In it, the writer upserts and deletes rows, appends the txn rows, and updates meta.head_seq.
    4. Serialisation runs in parallel. STEP text for the dirty entities and canonical JSON for RXD are produced in parallel with rayon at commit time, then handed to the writer.
    5. Session micro-operations. Each step of an interactive session, such as adding a sketch line or picking a point, is appended to session_op through the same writer and group commit. When the session finishes, its operations become one normal model transaction and the session row is marked committed. Cancelling a session marks it cancelled.
    6. Undo and redo are ordinary change sets. They update the state tables and toggle txn.undone.
    7. Checkpointing. WAL auto-checkpoint runs at about 4 MB. An explicit PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) follows each Save and each idle period of more than 30 s.

    Large operations. - Opening a project or importing a large IFC fills ifc_entity in a single transaction, using prepared statements and batched inserts. - Loading a 200 MB IFC4 file must not add more than 25 % to open time (NFR-PERF-001). If the user starts editing first, the bulk insert continues in the background, and recovery during that window falls back to the source IFC plus the journal.

    5. Durability Settings

    Setting Default Notes
    journal_mode WAL Readers never block the writer, which allows read-only access for diagnostics
    synchronous NORMAL With WAL, committed data survives an application crash. On power loss or an OS crash, at most the last group-commit window can be lost. FULL is available as a "maximum safety" preference, at a throughput cost.
    Group-commit window 250 ms Default upper bound on committed work at risk
    foreign_keys ON —
    page_size 8192 —
    cache_size −65536 (64 MiB) —

    Recovery-point objective (RPO): - Application crash: everything committed up to the last completed group commit, so normally less than 0.25 s of committed work at risk. - Power loss with NORMAL: at most about 1 s. - Interactive sessions in progress are covered too, to the same bound: their micro-operations are journaled (§6.5).

    Commands. live.flush() -> head_seq forces the pending group commit and returns once that sequence number is durable; scripts call it before an external step that must not lose work (DM-LIVE-003). live.settings.set(key, value) -> status changes one preference: synchronous (normal|full), group_commit_ms (50–2,000), location (user_data|beside_project), retention_days, retention_gb, quota_gb, undo_depth. Out-of-range values are refused with live.setting_out_of_range, and a new location takes effect at the next project open (DM-LIVE-014).

    6. Recovery

    6.1 Detecting an unclean shutdown

    At startup, and whenever a project is opened, Reviera scans the live-store directory. A store needs recovery when all of these are true: - meta.clean_shutdown = '0' - its lock is stale (§2) - head_seq > saved_seq, or the store belongs to an untitled project that was never saved

    6.2 Recovery dialog (UI)

    "Recover unsaved work" lists each recoverable project with: - the project name and path (or "Untitled") - the time of the last change - the number of unsaved changes - the last few undo labels, for example "Create Wall · Move · Edit Type"

    Actions per project:

    Action Result
    Restore (default) Opens the project from the live store. Its title shows "(recovered)".
    Restore as copy… Asks for a new file path, then restores into it
    Show changes Lists the unsaved transactions, with origin and time
    Discard Asks for confirmation inside the dialog, then moves the store to the recovery bin (kept 7 days)
    Decide later Leaves the store untouched

    Commands. recovery.list() -> [RecoverableProject] returns the rows of this dialog (store key, project name or "Untitled", path, last change time, unsaved-change count, last undo labels, open sessions). recovery.show_changes(store_key) -> [TxnSummary] lists the unsaved transactions with origin and time. recovery.discard(store_key) -> status moves the store to the recovery bin. Restore is recovery.restore (§6.3) (DM-LIVE-004).

    6.3 Restore procedure

    1. Open the database read/write and run PRAGMA integrity_check (or quick_check above 1 GB).
    2. If it passes, load state directly from ifc_entity and rxd_* into IfcOpenShell and the element DB. No replay is needed, because the tables are the materialised state. Then regenerate geometry in parallel, using cache_tessellation where geom_hash still matches.
    3. If it fails: - Fall back to the base IFC (meta.base_ifc_sha256, the file the session was opened from, if it is still present and its hash matches). - Replay the txn forward change sets from saved_seq + 1 up to the last readable row. - Report how far replay got, with the label and time of the last transaction recovered.
    4. Restore the undo history. Undo and redo stacks are rebuilt from txn, so Undo still works after recovery, back to the configured depth.
    5. Mark the project dirty. The title bar shows that it is unsaved; the user saves to write the IFC.
    6. Keep the old store. The pre-recovery store is moved to the recovery bin, and a new session store is created.

    Commands. recovery.restore(store_key, as_copy_path?) -> {model_id, report} runs this procedure. With as_copy_path the restored project is keyed to that new path. The report states whether the materialised state or the journal replay was used, and the last transaction recovered (DM-LIVE-005). live.history(since_seq?, origin?) -> [TxnSummary] lists the journal entries behind the rebuilt undo stack (DM-LIVE-006).

    6.4 What is not recovered

    • Changes after the last group commit, after power loss. With NORMAL, that is about 1 s at most.
    • Open modal dialogs and unconfirmed input: for example a half-typed value in an Edit Type dialog that was never applied. This UI state is not model data.

    6.5 Sketch and tool session recovery

    1. Recording a session. Entering sketch mode, or starting a multi-step tool, creates a session row. Its context records the active view, work plane, element type and tool options. - Every step is journaled as a micro-operation in session_op: adding a curve, moving a vertex, setting a slope arrow, picking a point, changing an option. - Micro-operations are in the tool's own vocabulary. They are not model change sets, because nothing has been committed to the model yet.
    2. Recovering a session. - The recovery dialog shows open sessions under their project, for example "Sketch for 'Floor 3' — 14 edits, last at 14:31:52". - After the model is restored, Reviera offers Resume sketch or Discard sketch. - Resume reopens the same view and re-enters the same tool. It replays the micro-operations to rebuild the sketch exactly, including the undo stack inside the sketch, and leaves the user in sketch mode, ready to finish or cancel.
    3. Sessions that can be resumed. These are sketch mode (floors, roofs, ceilings, openings, railings, stairs by sketch, filled and masking regions, crop boundaries), multi-click placement tools (wall chains, beam chains, duct and pipe runs), group-edit mode, in-place family editing, and Family Editor documents opened from a project. - A Family Editor document has its own live store and is recovered in the same way.
    4. When the context is missing. If the view or host element the session needs no longer exists in the restored model, the session can't be resumed. Its curves can still be exported as detail lines into a drafting view, so the geometry isn't lost.
    5. Tools must support replay. Each interactive tool declares a micro-operation schema and a replay function. This is a requirement on every tool in Chapters 3–5 that has a multi-step session (DM-LIVE-015).

    Commands. recovery.resume_session(store_key, session_id) -> status re-enters the tool and replays the session; it fails with recovery.context_missing when the view or host is gone. recovery.discard_session(store_key, session_id) -> status marks the session cancelled. recovery.export_session_curves(session_id, drafting_view_id?) -> view_id writes the session's curves as detail lines into the given drafting view, or into a new one named after the session; it is the only undoable command here (DM-LIVE-015).

    7. Save, Close and Housekeeping

    • Save writes IFC from memory, using the atomic save from Chapter 2a §9, then sets meta.saved_seq = head_seq and checkpoints.
    • Clean close sets clean_shutdown = '1'. The store is kept, as the history for time travel and as a fast-reopen cache (§8.1), until it falls outside the retention policy. A clean store whose project file no longer exists is deleted after 14 days.
    • Journal retention.
    • The journal is kept for time travel (§8.5), subject to a retention policy: by default 30 days or 5 GB per project, whichever comes first, and always at least the configured undo depth (default 200 transactions).
    • Older journal rows are removed in whole keyframe intervals, so every retained seq can still be reconstructed.
    • Snapshots the user has named are kept until the user deletes them.
    • VACUUM runs in the background when free pages exceed 25 %.
    • Disk quota. By default all live stores together may use up to 20 GB. The oldest clean stores are removed first, and stores that need recovery are never removed automatically.
    • Saving elsewhere. Save As or Save a copy re-keys the store to the new path; the old key is removed.

    8. Additional Uses

    1. Fast reopen. If a clean store exists and its base_ifc_sha256 and saved_seq match the project file, Reviera can open from the store without parsing STEP. The aim is at least 3× faster for large models. The file hash is always checked, so the IFC file stays authoritative.
    2. BIMserver working copies (Chapter 6). The live store is the offline working copy: base_entity and base_rxd hold the downloaded base revision for the three-way merge, and the live tables hold local edits. Offline work, crash recovery and sync therefore share one mechanism, and an offline session that crashes recovers with its merge base intact.
    3. Audit and diagnostics. txn.origin records who made each change (user, Lua script, add-in, MCP agent). This supports the "undo agent turn" feature (Chapter 1) and reports such as "what did the agent change?". Support bundles may include a redacted copy of the journal, with the user's consent.
    4. Read-only queries for tools. The store is opened read-only alongside the WAL, so external analysis tools and Lua scripts can query model data with SQL without blocking editing (§10).

    Commands. live.query(sql, params?) -> rows runs one read-only SQL statement on a separate read connection. Statements that write (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ATTACH, PRAGMA with a value) are refused with live.query.read_only. It needs the script/admin trust level (§10) and is not exposed over MCP by default.

    8.5 Time travel (history browser)

    Purpose. Lets the user browse the model's past states, compare them with the present, and bring back anything that was lost. This includes the ability to review and undo work done by scripts and AI agents.

    Reconstruction. - The state at any retained seq N is rebuilt by taking the nearest keyframe (a snapshot row) and applying the forward change sets from the journal. Starting from the current head and applying inverse change sets backwards is used instead when that path is shorter. - Keyframes are written: - at every Save - at session start - every 500 transactions or 30 minutes of editing - when the user asks (Mark snapshot, optionally named) - Building keyframes: they are compressed with zstd and written by the writer thread when it is idle. - Reconstruction runs in a background task, in parallel by sid range. It fills a read-only historical model: a separate in-memory model instance that never touches the live model.

    UI: History panel (dockable; Ribbon › View › Windows › History; shortcut Ctrl+Shift+H). - Timeline. The timeline lists transactions newest first, grouped by session and by save point. - Each row shows time, undo label, origin badge (User, Lua, Add-in, Agent, Sync) and the number of elements affected. - Filters: origin, command, element (all changes to the selected element), time range, and named snapshots only. - A scrubber along the top marks saves, syncs and named snapshots. - Preview. Selecting a row opens a historical view window of the active view as it was after that transaction. It has a banner, "Viewing history: 2026-10-12 14:31 · read-only", and the elements that differ from the current model are highlighted: added in green, changed in amber, deleted shown as ghosts. The view also offers Prev, Next and Return to present. - Actions:

    Action Result
    Compare with current A difference report listing elements added, changed or deleted and RXD documents changed, with parameter-level detail and a jump-to-element option
    Restore selected elements Copies the historical state of the chosen elements (and their dependent RXD, such as their tags) into the current model as one new undoable transaction, "Restore from history". Hosting and joins are re-resolved; conflicts are reported.
    Revert to this point Applies the inverse of every later transaction as one new undoable transaction. Nothing is lost: the reverted transactions stay in the journal.
    Revert a single transaction or agent turn Applies one transaction's inverse, or one agent turn's inverses, if later transactions don't depend on it. Otherwise it lists the dependent transactions and offers to revert them all together.
    Save as copy at this point Writes the historical model to a new .ifc file
    Mark snapshot Names the current or selected point
    - Scope. Time travel covers what the live store retains (§7). Older history comes from saved files and backups. In BIMserver mode, the server's revisions and shared snapshots join the same timeline (§8.6).
    - Performance target. Reconstructing a state up to 500 transactions from a keyframe on a 200 MB model shows the historical view in 3 s or less on an 8-core workstation.

    Commands. history.list(since?, until?, origin?, command?, element?) -> [TxnSummary] fills the timeline with its filters. history.open_view(seq, view_id) -> historical_view_id opens the read-only historical view. history.compare(seq_a, seq_b?) -> DiffReport compares two points, or one point with the present when seq_b is omitted. history.restore_elements(seq, element_ids[]) -> report, history.revert_to(seq) -> report and history.revert_txn(seq | agent_turn_id, include_dependents?) -> report each make one new undoable transaction. history.save_copy_at(seq, path) -> status writes the historical model as .ifc (DM-LIVE-017). history.mark_snapshot(label?, seq?) -> seq writes a keyframe at the head, or at seq, and names it; named snapshots are exempt from retention (DM-LIVE-018).

    8.6 BIMserver integration: unified timeline and shared snapshots

    Accepted by the owner, 2026-10-12 (formerly OD4 and OD5).

    8.6.1 Unified timeline

    • What it shows. In BIMserver mode, the History panel shows one combined timeline, ordered by time, of:
    • local transactions
    • local saves
    • sync points (get latest, check in)
    • server revisions by every user
    • shared snapshots (§8.6.2)
    • Lanes. Each entry has a lane marker: Local, Server or Snapshot. Lane filters show any combination; Server only gives the separate-track view.
    • Server revision entries. Each shows the revision number, author, date and check-in comment. The list comes from ServiceInterface.getAllRevisionsOfProject(poid), which is confirmed in the public BIMserver source. It is refreshed when a new-revision notification arrives.
    • Where local work sits. Local transactions appear between the server revision they were based on (meta.base_roid) and the next sync. Sync points link local work to the revisions it produced, so it is visible which local changes went into which server revision.
    • Actions on a server revision:
    • View: a read-only historical view. The revision is downloaded on demand, with its embedded RXD, and cached as a keyframe (snapshot.reason = 'server_revision', with roid stored in label), so viewing it again is instant.
    • Compare with the current model, or with any other timeline entry
    • Restore selected elements into the current model, as one new undoable transaction
    • Save as copy
    • Show changes: a summary, revision against its predecessor, by element
    • Reverting to a server revision. This is done locally as one transaction: the difference between the current model and that revision is applied. It reaches the server at the next sync, as an ordinary new revision. History is never rewritten on the server.
    • Permissions. Users only see revisions their BIMserver account can read.

    Commands. history.list_server_revisions(since?, author?) -> [RevisionSummary] lists the Server lane. history.open_server_revision(roid, view_id?) -> historical_view_id downloads (or reuses the cached keyframe of) a revision and opens it read-only. history.revert_to_server_revision(roid) -> report applies the difference as one local transaction (DM-LIVE-019).

    8.6.2 Shared snapshots on BIMserver

    • Purpose. Lets a user publish a named snapshot, for example "Option B before client review", so that teammates can see it, compare against it and restore from it. Unlike a check-in, publishing a snapshot doesn't change the project's latest revision.
    • Default transport: Extended Data. The snapshot is attached to the server revision it was based on. The calls are confirmed in BIMserver's public ServiceInterface: 1. Register the extended-data schema org.reviera.snapshot/1.0 once (addExtendedDataSchema, looked up by getExtendedDataSchemaByName). 2. Upload the snapshot, a .ifczip with embedded RXD, written from the historical model at that seq (uploadFile). 3. Attach it with addExtendedDataToRevision(base_roid, {schemaId, fileId, title}). The title is the snapshot label. 4. Teammates list snapshots with getAllExtendedDataOfRevisionAndSchema(roid, schemaId) for each revision in the timeline, and download one with getFile when they open it.
    • Snapshot metadata. A small JSON manifest, stored in the IFC's Reviera_Manifest and repeated in the extended-data title and description: label, description, author, created time, local seq, base roid, and the Reviera version that wrote it.
    • Optional: publish as a browsable project. For snapshots that should open in BIMserver's own viewers and query tools, Reviera can check the snapshot in as a revision of a companion project, by default named <Project> [Snapshots] (created on demand with project-creation rights). It deliberately does not use a sub-project, because BIMserver merges sub-projects into the parent's latest model. The companion project is recorded in the main project's RXD document project/links with the role snapshots.
    • Snapshots from other users appear in the Snapshot lane, showing their author. The actions are View, Compare, Restore selected elements, and Save as copy. A snapshot shared by someone else can't be edited in place; it is opened as a copy.
    • Deleting. Authors (and project administrators) can withdraw a shared snapshot. The public ServiceInterface has no method for deleting extended data. In the extended-data transport, withdrawing therefore attaches a tombstone extended-data item (schema org.reviera.snapshot-withdrawn/1.0, holding the withdrawn snapshot's file id) to the same revision. Clients hide snapshots that have a tombstone. Administrators can purge withdrawn files on the server, outside Reviera. In the companion project, the revision is kept, because BIMserver revisions can't be deleted, but it is tagged withdrawn in its comment.
    • Size guard. Snapshots larger than a configurable limit (default 500 MB) ask the user for confirmation, and suggest the companion project, where BIMserver stores objects instead of whole files.

    Commands. snapshot.publish(seq | snapshot_label, label, description?, target: extended_data|companion_project) -> {roid?, extended_data_oid?} publishes a point of the timeline. snapshot.list_shared(roid?) -> [SharedSnapshot] lists the Snapshot lane, hiding tombstoned items. snapshot.open_shared(snapshot_ref, mode: view|copy) -> historical_view_id | model_id opens one read-only, or as an editable copy. snapshot.withdraw(snapshot_ref) -> status attaches the tombstone; only the author or a project administrator may call it (DM-LIVE-020).

    9. Concurrency and Multi-core Notes

    • One writer thread per open project. SQLite access is single-writer, and the writer owns its connection.
    • Parallel work happens before the writer. Change-set serialisation, compression and hashing run in parallel with rayon, so the writer does only inserts.
    • Read-only connections for diagnostics and SQL queries use separate connections in WAL mode and never take the write lock.
    • Recovery loads table data in parallel chunks by sid range, then regenerates in parallel as described in Chapter 2 §2.6.

    10. Security and Privacy

    • The live store contains unsaved project data in plain form. It inherits the user's file permissions: 0600 on POSIX, and the user's ACL on Windows.
    • The params column never holds credentials. Commands mark secret parameters in their schema, and those values are written as "<redacted>".
    • Lua and MCP may read the live store only through the commands in §12. Raw SQL is available only to callers holding the script or admin command permission class (Lua at trust level trusted or native, DM-LUA-007; MCP tokens granted those classes), and only read-only.
    • Encryption at rest: see §10.1.

    10.1 Encryption at rest

    • Engine. SQLCipher (AES-256 page encryption, HMAC-SHA512 page authentication, PBKDF2 key derivation), through rusqlite with the bundled-sqlcipher-vendored-openssl feature. The live store, its WAL file, the session journal and the snapshots are all encrypted. The -shm file contains no row data.
    • Default: on, whenever an OS credential store is available.
    • Keys.
    • Each live store gets a random 256-bit key at creation.
    • The key is held in the OS credential store, accessed with the keyring crate: Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, or Secret Service/KWallet on Linux. It is stored under the store's key name.
    • Recovery and time travel unlock the store with it, without asking the user.
    • Fallbacks.
    • If no credential store is available (for example a headless Linux session), the user can set a recovery passphrase. The key is then derived with PBKDF2 at SQLCipher's default iteration count. The user can also turn encryption off for that machine; the status bar indicator then shows "Recovery data not encrypted".
    • Organisations can require encryption by policy setting. Reviera then refuses to create a store without a usable key: editing continues, and the indicator shows the store as unavailable.
    • Losing the key. If the key is lost (credential store reset, or passphrase forgotten), the live store can't be read. The recovery dialog says so and offers to Discard. The project's saved IFC file is unaffected.
    • Scope. Encryption applies to the live store only. Encrypting .ifc deliverables is out of scope, and remains for OS or file-system encryption or for document-management systems.
    • Performance. The overhead must stay within the targets in §4. SQLCipher typically adds 5–15 % to I/O-bound work, which the writer thread absorbs.

    Commands. live.encryption.status() -> {enabled, key_source, policy} reports the current state for the status-bar indicator. live.encryption.set(enabled, key_source: os_store|passphrase, passphrase?) -> status re-keys the store (SQLCipher rekey) on the writer thread; the passphrase is a secret parameter and is never journaled. Turning encryption off is refused with live.encryption.required_by_policy when policy requires it (DM-LIVE-016).

    Acceptance criteria - [ ] Kill the process (SIGKILL / Task Manager) 1 s after creating a wall. On restart the recovery dialog lists the project, and Restore shows the wall. - [ ] After recovery, Undo removes the wall. - [ ] An untitled project with 20 edits, killed, is recoverable and can be saved as a new file. - [ ] Corrupt the .rvlive file (truncate it to half its size). Recovery falls back to base IFC plus journal replay and reports the last recovered change. - [ ] Opening the same project in a second instance offers read-only mode or a copy. - [ ] The UI frame time is not affected by live-store writes during a 10,000-element array operation: the 95th-percentile frame time stays within 10 % of the time with the live store disabled. - [ ] The params column contains no BIMserver password after a login command. - [ ] Kill the process halfway through sketching a floor boundary (6 lines drawn). After restoring and choosing Resume sketch, the 6 lines are back in sketch mode on the same view, and Undo inside the sketch removes the 6th. - [ ] Open the .rvlive file with plain sqlite3: it fails with "file is not a database". Recovery inside Reviera works with no prompt. - [ ] With the credential store entry deleted, the recovery dialog explains that the data can't be decrypted and offers Discard. The saved IFC file opens normally. - [ ] Let an MCP agent make 12 changes in one turn, then the user makes 3 more. In History, Revert agent turn undoes the agent's changes as one new transaction and keeps the user's 3 changes, or lists the dependencies if they conflict. - [ ] Select a wall deleted 2 hours ago and choose Restore selected elements. It comes back with its hosted door and tag, as one undoable step. - [ ] In BIMserver mode with 3 server revisions by two users, the History panel shows them interleaved with local transactions. Server only shows just the 3. Viewing revision 2 opens a read-only historical view, and viewing it again needs no download. - [ ] User A publishes snapshot "Option B". The project's latest revision is unchanged. User B sees "Option B (A)" in the Snapshot lane after refreshing, and can compare it with B's current model. - [ ] Publishing to a companion project creates <Project> [Snapshots] with the snapshot as a revision. The main project's latest revision and its sub-project structure are unchanged. - [ ] After pulling power on a test VM with synchronous=NORMAL, at most the last 1 s of committed changes is missing, and the store passes integrity_check.

    14. Open Questions and Deviations

    • ~~DM-LIVE-OD1~~ Accepted (owner, 2026-10-12): sketch and tool session recovery, specified in §6.5 (DM-LIVE-015).
    • ~~DM-LIVE-OD2~~ Accepted (owner, 2026-10-12): encryption at rest with SQLCipher, on by default, specified in §10.1 (DM-LIVE-016).
    • ~~DM-LIVE-OD3~~ Accepted (owner, 2026-10-12): time travel through the History panel, specified in §8.5 (DM-LIVE-017/018).
    • ~~DM-LIVE-OD4~~ Accepted (owner, 2026-10-12): one combined timeline that includes BIMserver revisions, with lane filters that also give the separate-track view (§8.6.1, DM-LIVE-019).
    • ~~DM-LIVE-OD5~~ Accepted (owner, 2026-10-12): shared snapshots on BIMserver (§8.6.2, DM-LIVE-020).
    • DM-LIVE-OD6: if a future BIMserver version adds a way to delete extended data, snapshot.withdraw should use it instead of the tombstone. For now, withdrawing works through tombstones (§8.6.2).
    • Implementation note (2026-10-12, first build). The core keeps edited element state apart from the IFC population until Save, so the materialised state has two parts: ifc_entity (the IFC graph as of the last open or Save) and an additional element table (current elements as JSON). txn.origin stores the full origin as JSON, so session-scoped undo survives recovery. Restore rebuilds the IFC from ifc_entity, loads element, and marks the differences for the next Save. Encryption (DM-LIVE-016), session journaling (DM-LIVE-015), housekeeping (DM-LIVE-010) and time travel are not built yet. In the truncation test, nothing could be read from a half-truncated small store, so recovery returned the base IFC and reported the damage; reading the journal more robustly is follow-up work.
    • Deviation from the reference. The reference offers save reminders and rotating backups. Reviera adds continuous transactional persistence, and keeps the reference's numbered backups (Chapter 6, maintenance) as an independent safety net.

    3CHChapter 3: Architectural Modeling and Editing Tools

    Area code: ARC · Primary source: research/02_architecture_modeling.md · Target architecture: TECH_STACK.md Functional reference: Revit 2026 behaviour, with the 2027 changes applied where they differ (most importantly, there is no Options Bar).

    This chapter specifies how Reviera creates and edits the building model. It covers datums, walls, inserts, curtain systems, slabs, roofs, circulation, openings, rooms and areas, free-form and site elements, the general modify tools, groups, constraints and selection. It also defines the geometry algorithms that turn parametric elements into OpenCASCADE (OCCT) solids: wall joins and layer cleanup, layer wrapping, roof generation, stair and railing generation, shape editing, boolean cuts and room boundary computation. Those algorithms are written at implementation depth.

    3.0 Conventions used in this chapter

    3.0.1 Units, tolerances and coordinates

    • All lengths in the core are stored in metres as f64; angles are stored in radians. Display units come from the project settings (DM chapter). Values quoted here in mm or feet are display equivalents.
    • Model tolerances, used by every algorithm in this chapter unless one says otherwise:
    Name Value Use
    TOL_POINT 0.05 mm Two points are coincident
    TOL_ANGLE 1e-6 rad Two directions are parallel
    TOL_JOIN 1 mm + half the other wall's width Searching for wall-end join candidates
    TOL_ROOM_SNAP 0.5 mm Vertex merging in the room-boundary arrangement
    TOL_SHORT 0.8 mm Shortest curve allowed in a sketch or location line ("element too short" error)
    OCCT_FUZZY 1e-5 m Fuzzy value passed to OCCT Boolean operations (BOPAlgo_Options::SetFuzzyValue)
    • The model uses a right-handed coordinate system: +Z is up, project north is +Y in the project coordinate system, and true north is applied through the site's rotation (DM chapter).
    • "Left of the drawing direction". For a curve traced from start to end and viewed from above, left is the side reached by rotating the tangent by +90° about +Z.

    3.0.2 Requirement blocks

    Feature blocks follow the template in 00_conventions.md §5. Each Commands line names registry commands. All of them are undoable unless they are marked (query). They are exposed automatically to the UI, to Lua (reviera.<domain>.<verb>(...)) and to MCP. The following conventions apply to every command signature in this chapter: - curve is a 2D or 3D curve value: Line{p0,p1}, Arc{center,radius,a0,a1,normal}, Arc3{p0,pm,p1}, Ellipse{center,rx,ry,rot,a0,a1}, Spline{ctrl,knots,degree} or CurveLoop[...]. - loops is a list of closed CurveLoops. The first loop is the outer loop and the rest are holes. Commands may accept several outer loops when the feature allows it. - level_ref is the element ID of a level. host_ref is an element ID, optionally followed by a face reference (elem#face:<stable-face-key>). - ? marks an optional parameter. Every create command returns the new element's element_id, and those that create more than one element return [element_id].

    3.0.3 Regeneration model (summary)

    The Rust core keeps a regeneration graph. Its nodes are elements and its directed edges mean "the output of A is an input of B". Every feature block lists the edges it adds. The detailed ordering and parallelism rules are in §3.15. The edge kinds are:

    Edge kind Meaning
    datum The element reads the elevation, plane or curve of a level, grid, reference plane or work plane
    join Two elements share a join node, and both read the resolved join topology
    attach The element's extent is clipped by another element's geometry
    host A hosted element reads its host's placement, and the host reads the insert's cutting geometry
    cut A Boolean subtraction of one element's tool solid from another element's body
    bound A room, area or space reads bounding geometry
    type An instance reads its type's parameters (compound structure, layout rules)
    group A group instance reads its group type definition
    constraint A constraint node reads and writes references of several elements
    sketch-lock A sketch line follows a picked edge of another element

    3.0.4 IFC conventions

    • The default schema is IFC4 ADD2 TC1. Where IFC4X3 offers a better entity or enumeration, the IFC4X3 mapping is given as well, marked (4X3).
    • Every physical element is contained in its storey through IfcRelContainedInSpatialStructure. Elements on a reference (non-story) level are contained in the nearest story level at or below that level, and the true reference level is recorded in RXD element data (placement).
    • Every type is linked to its occurrences through IfcRelDefinesByType, and materials are linked through IfcRelAssociatesMaterial.
    • IFC keeps element geometry and representations, types, material layer sets, openings and voids (IfcRelVoidsElement / IfcRelFillsElement), IfcRelSpaceBoundary, standard Pset_* / Qto_* sets, and the values of user-visible parameters (property sets defined by the DM chapter).
    • Reviera Extension Data (RXD) keeps everything else. The carrier, encoding, geometry hash and reconciliation rules are defined in spec/02a_extension_data_format.md; this chapter only says which RXD object holds each piece of data, using two forms:
    • "RXD element data (<kind>)" is data owned by one element (or one type): its recipe (recipe.wall, recipe.roof, recipe.stair, recipe.railing, recipe.curtain_grid, recipe.toposolid, …), its sketch, and the constraints and join overrides it owns. For types this is the type-level RXD data.
    • "RXD document <name>" is project-level data. This chapter uses model/constraints (constraints between elements, attach relations, Join Geometry and Cut Geometry pairs), model/groups, model/rooms (room and area computation settings, area schemes and rules, unplaced rooms), model/selection_sets, model/parts (part divisions and merges), project/settings (site settings), families/<id> (family recipes, including in-place families and masses) and the views documents (colour schemes; DOC chapter).
    Data written by this chapter Where it goes
    Sketch curves, per-curve properties, slope arrows, span direction, pick-and-lock targets, shape-edit modifiers of floors and roofs RXD element data (sketch) on the host
    Wall location-line choice and flip, per-end allow/disallow join, per-end wrap override, wall profile, hosted-wall relation and offset RXD element data (recipe.wall)
    Join type, join order and display at a join node; attach top/base relations; Join Geometry / Cut Geometry / Join Roof pairs; alignment locks, locked dimensions, EQ; Moves With Nearby/Grids links RXD document model/constraints
    Compound-structure flags (wraps, variable, structural, exact priority), core boundaries, vertical regions, type sweeps and reveals, stacked-wall rows, curtain layout rules, railing rail and baluster tables, stair run and landing types RXD type data (recipe.compound, recipe.stacked_wall, recipe.curtain_type, recipe.railing_type, recipe.stair_type)
    Datum extents (3D and per-view 2D), bubbles, elbows, end locks, scope box assignment, grid-axis identity RXD element data (recipe.datum) on the datum or IfcGrid
    Stair runs, landings, supports, multistory connections RXD element data (recipe.stair)
    Curtain grid and mullion instance layout RXD element data (recipe.curtain_grid)
    Toposolid points, split lines, sub-divisions, excavation and grading links, contour settings RXD element data (recipe.toposolid)
    Work-plane host and reference-level hosting of any element RXD element data (placement)
    Group types, exclusions, array associations RXD document model/groups
    Room/area settings, area schemes and rules, unplaced rooms RXD document model/rooms
    Colour schemes RXD views documents (DOC chapter)
    Saved selection sets RXD document model/selection_sets
    Part identity, parent, exclusion, overrides and face offsets RXD element data (recipe.part) on each part
    Part divisions (curves, references, gap, profile) and merges RXD document model/parts
    Site settings (contour defaults, section graphics, property-line angle format) and toposolid smooth shading RXD document project/settings (section site)
    Flip state (facing, hand, mirrored) of family instances RXD element data (placement)

    All references are IFC GlobalIds, in the reference forms defined in 02a_extension_data_format.md §6.2. Sub-element references use named sub-references, such as #end:1, #face:core.ext or #axis:<uuid>, never indices. - Edits by other tools. When the geometry hash in an element's RXD data no longer matches its IFC representation, or the element has no RXD data, Reviera treats the element as described in 02a_extension_data_format.md §7: it is either stale (the user chooses between keeping the external geometry and regenerating) or non-parametric. - In the IFC files Reviera writes, every element has an Axis or FootPrint representation where one makes sense, plus a Body representation. The Body uses the simplest valid form in this order of preference: IfcExtrudedAreaSolid, then IfcBooleanClippingResult, then IfcFacetedBrep / IfcAdvancedBrep, then IfcPolygonalFaceSet. On load, the parametric definition in RXD takes precedence (unless it is stale) over the explicit body. The body is a cache that lets other tools read the file.

    3.1 Shared interaction model

    The behaviours in this section are implemented once, in the tool framework, and are reused by every tool in this chapter.

    3.1.1 Tool framework and contextual tabs

    ID: ARC-TOOL-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §1, §2.1, §2.4, §17.1 · screenshots/architecture/modify_walls_contextual_ribbon.png

    Purpose. Every creation or edit tool runs on one shared state machine and presents its options in one shared, consistent way.

    Workflow. 1. The user starts a tool from the ribbon, a shortcut, the Lua/MCP command, Create Similar, or Repeat last command. 2. The tool enters Pick-type. The Type Selector defaults to the last type used with this tool in the session. 3. The tool enters Options. The contextual tab Modify | Place <Element> opens, and the Properties palette shows the New <Element> instance defaults. 4. The tool enters Input. Clicks, typed values and picks are collected, and a live preview is drawn. 5. The tool enters Commit. One transaction is created, the regeneration graph runs, and the tool returns to Input so that the user can place again. 6. Esc once cancels the current input chain. Esc a second time, or pressing Modify, ends the tool.

    UI. - The contextual tab always contains the Select, Properties, Clipboard, Geometry, Modify, View, Measure and Create panels. It then adds the Draw gallery and any tool-specific panels (Placement, Tag, Constraint, Mode). - The Draw gallery offers: Line, Rectangle, Inscribed Polygon, Circumscribed Polygon, Circle, Start-End-Radius Arc, Center-Ends Arc, Tangent End Arc, Fillet Arc, Spline, Ellipse, Partial Ellipse, Pick Lines, and Pick Faces / Pick Walls. A tool enables only the entries it supports. - Selecting existing elements shows Modify | <Category> with Mode (Edit Sketch, Edit Profile, Edit Type, as applicable) and element-specific panels. - There is no Options Bar. Every tool option is either a control on the contextual tab (toggle, numeric field or drop-down) or a field in the Properties palette's New <Element> block.

    Behaviour & rules. - Tool options are remembered per tool for the session. The user can choose to persist them per user in the user settings file (reviera-user.toml; UI chapter). - Every tool can be invoked in two orders: select, then tool (the tool acts on the current selection at once) and tool, then select. In the second order the user confirms with Enter or Finish. - Each commit is a single undo step. A multi-step tool, such as sketch mode or the group editor, uses a transaction group that collapses into one undo step on Finish and is rolled back completely on Cancel. - A tool descriptor declares its panels, options, input phases and command bindings. The UI tab is built from that descriptor, so tools added from Lua get the same UI treatment.

    Data (IFC mapping). None. Session state only.

    Commands. tool.start(command_id, type_id?, preset_args?) -> session_id, tool.cancel(), tool.finish() -> (), tool.set_option(tool_id? (default: active tool), key, value) -> (), tool.repeat_last() -> session_id. Placement itself always goes through the element-specific create commands, so scripts and agents never need the interactive tool.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Every placement tool in this chapter opens a contextual tab, and no control is shown outside the tab or the Properties palette. - [ ] Placing three walls in a row and pressing Ctrl+Z three times removes them one at a time. - [ ] Cancelling a sketch session leaves the model byte-identical to its state before the session (comparing the GlobalId set and the attribute hashes). - [ ] A tool option changed in one invocation keeps its value in the next invocation in the same session.

    3.1.2 Type and instance properties

    ID: ARC-TOOL-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.2

    Purpose. Every element exposes type parameters, which are shared by all instances of the type, and instance parameters, which belong to one element.

    Workflow. The Type Selector at the top of the Properties palette changes the type of the selected elements, or the type that a running tool will place. Edit Type opens the Type Properties dialog, which offers Duplicate, Rename, Load (for loadable families) and a preview pane.

    Behaviour & rules. - System types (walls, floors, roofs, ceilings, stairs, railings, ramps, curtain walls and systems, toposolids, levels, grids) are defined in the project. - Loadable types (doors, windows, components, columns, profiles, balusters, panels, mullion profiles) come from Reviera family files (DM chapter). - Changing the type of a placed element keeps the element's reference geometry: the location line for walls, the boundary for slabs and the insertion point for families. - A type change that cannot be applied, such as a door type that is wider than its host segment, is rejected with a warning that names the elements involved.

    Data (IFC mapping). IfcTypeObject subtypes linked through IfcRelDefinesByType. Type parameters are held in property sets on the type, and instance parameters in property sets on the occurrence. Details are in the DM chapter.

    Commands. element.set_type(element_ids, type_id), type.duplicate(type_id, new_name) -> type_id, type.rename(type_id, name) -> (), type.set_param(type_id, param, value) -> (), element.set_param(element_ids, name, value).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Changing a wall's type from 200 mm to 300 mm with Location Line = Finish Face: Exterior leaves the exterior face where it was. - [ ] Editing a type parameter regenerates every instance of that type in a single transaction.

    3.1.3 Sketch mode

    ID: ARC-SKCH-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.3, §17.2 · screenshots/architecture/roof_footprint_sketch_mode.png

    Purpose. A modal editing session for elements whose shape comes from user-drawn curves rather than from a single click.

    Elements that use sketch mode: floors, sketched ceilings, footprint and extrusion roofs, soffits, openings (shaft, vertical, by face, dormer), railing paths, stair and ramp sketches (boundary, riser, path), split face, toposolid boundaries and sub-divisions, wall elevation profiles, property lines, multi-segment grids, and area or room-separation boundaries when they are edited as a set.

    Workflow. 1. The user starts a sketch-based tool, or chooses Edit Sketch / Edit Boundary / Edit Profile on an existing element. 2. The view enters sketch mode. All non-sketch elements are drawn in the half-tone "edit mode" colour, which the user can configure, and they still snap. Sketch curves are drawn in the sketch colour (magenta by default). 3. The contextual tab shows the Draw gallery, the sketch-element pickers relevant to the host (Boundary Line, Slope Arrow, Span Direction, Riser, Stair Path, Symbolic Line and so on) and a Mode panel with Finish (✓) and Cancel (✗). 4. The user draws, picks or edits curves. Selecting a sketch curve shows its per-curve properties in the Properties palette. 5. Finish validates the sketch (ARC-SKCH-002). If the sketch is valid, the element is regenerated and the session closes. If it is invalid, a dialog lists the problems and highlights the offending curves, and the session stays open.

    UI. The draw options Chain, Offset, Radius (fillet corners while chaining) and Lock (for Pick tools) appear as contextual-tab controls. Right-click › Snap Overrides › Close closes an open chain, and Tab cycles between the candidate closing points.

    Behaviour & rules. - A sketch is a child model owned by the host element: sketch curves, slope arrows, span direction symbols, riser and boundary curves and the stair path. It is stored with the host and keeps stable IDs across edits, so that dimensions and locks can refer to sketch curves. - Pick-and-lock. A curve created with Pick Walls, Pick Lines or Pick Roof Edges while Lock is on gets a sketch-lock dependency on the picked edge or face. When the source moves, the sketch curve is recomputed and the host regenerates. If the source is deleted, the lock is dropped silently and the curve keeps its last position. - Pick Walls uses the wall's finish face on the side the cursor is on, unless Extend into wall (to core) is on, in which case it uses the core face. The Offset value is measured from that face. - Tab while hovering a pick candidate selects the connected chain of the same kind, for example all walls joined end to end. - The sketch session uses a transaction group (ARC-TOOL-001), so Cancel discards every change.

    Data (IFC mapping). The sketch is stored as RXD element data (sketch) on the host. Each curve has a stable key, its geometry, its role (boundary, slope arrow, riser and so on), its per-curve properties and an optional lock target (GlobalId plus face key). The resulting geometry is exported normally: for example, a floor boundary becomes the IfcArbitraryProfileDefWithVoids of its extrusion.

    Commands. sketch.begin(host_id, role?) -> session_id, sketch.add_curve(session_id, curve, role?, props?) -> curve_key, sketch.pick(session_id, ref, offset?, lock?, chain?) -> [curve_key], sketch.edit_curve(session_id, curve_key, curve?, props?), sketch.delete_curve(session_id, curve_key), sketch.finish(session_id) -> element_id, sketch.cancel(session_id). Every create command that takes loops creates the sketch implicitly, so a non-interactive caller never needs a session.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A floor sketched with Pick Walls and Lock on follows the wall when the wall is moved 500 mm, and its area updates. - [ ] Cancelling an Edit Boundary session restores the previous boundary exactly. - [ ] Finish on an open loop leaves the session open and highlights the open ends.

    3.1.4 Sketch validation

    ID: ARC-SKCH-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.3

    Purpose. A deterministic way to decide whether a sketch can produce an element, with messages that tell the user what to fix.

    Behaviour & rules. The validator runs these checks in order on the curves with the "boundary" role: 1. Short curves. Any curve shorter than TOL_SHORT is an error. 2. Near-axis curves. A line within 0.2° of the X or Y axis of the view or work plane, but not exactly on it, raises a warning ("Line is slightly off axis"). This is not an error. 3. Overlaps. Two curves that share a positive-length piece are an error ("Curves overlap"). 4. Loop building. Endpoints are merged within TOL_POINT, and a graph is built in which curves are edges. Every vertex must have degree exactly 2. A vertex of degree 1 means an open loop, and a vertex of degree 3 or more means a branch. Both are errors ("Curves must form closed loops"). 5. Self-intersection. No two curves may intersect except at a shared endpoint. Reviera uses exact line/arc intersection; ellipses and splines are subdivided adaptively to TOL_POINT. An intersection is an error ("Curves intersect"). 6. Nesting. The loops are classified by containment. At even depth (0, 2, …) a loop is an outer boundary, and at odd depth it is a hole. An element type that allows only one outer loop (for example a roof by footprint) reports "Only one outer boundary is allowed" when it finds more. 7. Role-specific rules. - An extrusion roof needs exactly one open chain. - Stair and ramp sketches need exactly two non-touching boundary chains and at least one riser. - A railing path needs exactly one connected chain, open or closed. - A slope arrow's tail must lie on a boundary curve. - There may be at most one span direction symbol.

    Loop orientation is normalised on Finish: outer loops counter-clockwise and holes clockwise, seen from the sketch-plane normal.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A square with one side drawn 0.01 mm short reports an open loop at exactly that vertex. - [ ] A loop that has a hole loop inside a second hole loop produces an "island" outer region, so a floor with a nested island has two solid regions. - [ ] A figure-eight sketch is rejected with "Curves intersect".

    3.1.5 Per-curve sketch properties and slope arrows

    ID: ARC-SKCH-003 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.3, §7.1, §7.3, §7.4

    Purpose. Sketch curves carry parameters that shape the 3D result, such as slopes, overhangs and offsets.

    Behaviour & rules. - Floor and ceiling boundary curves: Defines Slope (bool), Slope (rise/run or angle) and Offset from Base (m). At most one curve may define slope. Two parallel curves whose Offset from Base values differ also define the slab plane. - Roof footprint curves: Defines Roof Slope (bool), Slope, Overhang (m, positive outward), Plate Offset from Base (m), Offset from Roof Base (m) and Extend into wall (to core) (bool). - Slope arrow (a two-point sketch element whose tail lies on a boundary curve): - Specify is either HeightAtTail or Slope. - With HeightAtTail, the arrow has Level at Tail, Height Offset at Tail, Level at Head and Height Offset at Head. - With Slope, the arrow has Level at Tail, Height Offset at Tail and Slope. - The arrow defines a plane. The plane contains the tail point at the tail height, rises along the arrow's direction, and its contour lines (lines of equal height) run at right angles to the arrow. - A boundary curve that carries a slope arrow cannot also be slope-defining. In roofs, slope arrows are used for dormer cheeks, four-sided gables and similar cases. - Span direction (structural decks; STR chapter) is a symbol curve that records an orientation and takes no other part in geometry. - Validation. Contradictory definitions, for example a slope arrow and a slope-defining curve that cover the same slab, are an error on Finish.

    Data (IFC mapping). These properties are stored per curve in RXD element data (sketch). The resulting tilt and faces are written as explicit geometry.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A floor with a single slope-defining curve at 2% produces a top face that rises 2 cm per metre measured at right angles to that curve. - [ ] A slope arrow from tail height 0 to head height 1.0 m over a 4 m arrow length gives a plane with a slope of 25%.

    3.1.6 Temporary dimensions

    ID: ARC-DIM-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.4, §15.1

    Purpose. On-the-fly dimensions that show where an element is and let the user drive its position by typing a value.

    Workflow. 1. While an element is being placed, or when exactly one element is selected, Reviera shows temporary dimensions to the nearest parallel references on each principal side. 2. The user clicks the dimension text, types a value and presses Enter. The selected element moves, and the reference at the other end stays where it is. 3. The user can drag a witness-line grip to another reference, or click the grip repeatedly to cycle through the candidate references on the same element (for walls: face, centreline, core face, core centre). 4. The Make permanent icon below a temporary dimension turns it into a permanent dimension (DOC chapter).

    UI. Text size and background (opaque or transparent) are set in Options › Graphics. The default references are set in Manage › Additional Settings › Temporary Dimensions: walls measure to Centerlines, Center of Core, Faces or Faces of Core, and doors and windows measure to Centerlines or Openings.

    Behaviour & rules. - Reference search. The candidates are references (faces, centrelines, datum planes and reference planes) that are parallel to the element's reference within TOL_ANGLE and visible in the view. Reviera chooses the closest candidate on each side within 30 m, and falls back to the nearest grid or level. - For a hosted insert, Reviera measures along the host wall to the nearest perpendicular walls or openings, as set in the Temporary Dimensions settings. - Editing a temporary dimension runs a move command, so it respects pins, constraints and hosting (§3.12).

    Commands. dim.temporary_query(element_id, view_id) -> [TempDim] (query). Driving a temporary dimension issues element.move or wall.set_location. dim.make_permanent(view_id, temporary_dimension_ref | {ref_a, ref_b}) -> dimension_id creates the permanent dimension.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Selecting a door shows dimensions from the door centreline to the nearest perpendicular walls on both sides. Typing a new value moves the door along its host. - [ ] Clicking a wall-reference grip repeatedly cycles through at least four references and then wraps around.

    3.1.7 Listening dimensions

    ID: ARC-DIM-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §2.4, §11.3 · web: Use Listening Dimensions

    Purpose. Typed precise input while drawing.

    Workflow. 1. The user starts a line-based tool and clicks the first point. A listening dimension (the live length, radius or angle shown next to the rubber-band preview) follows the cursor. 2. The user types a digit, a sign or a decimal separator. An inline input box opens next to the cursor, pre-filled with the typed character, and the preview freezes its direction. 3. Enter commits the value; Esc closes the box without committing and leaves the tool waiting for the second point; Backspace edits the text. 4. In a chain tool (walls, lines, sketch lines with Chain), the committed end point becomes the next start point and the box closes until the next keystroke.

    UI. The box shows the value in display units with the unit symbol of the project's length or angle format. The listening dimension itself is drawn in the temporary-dimension style (ARC-DIM-001).

    Behaviour & rules. - After the first click of a line-based input (lines, arcs, polygons by radius, circle radius, ellipse radii, offsets, move and copy distances), typing a numeric key opens an inline input box next to the cursor. - Enter commits the value along the current cursor direction. - Which quantity. The box drives the primary linear quantity of the step: line length; chord length for the second point of a three-point arc; radius for circles, polygons and centre-end arcs; distance for Move, Copy and Offset. When a step has no linear quantity (for example the sweep of a centre-end arc after its radius is fixed), the box takes an angle in the project's angle format. - Direction. The direction is the cursor direction at the moment the box opened, after snapping and any orthogonal constraint (Shift, or Constrain on Move and Copy). Moving the mouse while the box is open does not change it. - The input accepts the project's display units and these shorthands: imperial 8 6 means 8'-6"; 8'6", 2500 (in project units) and expressions such as 1200+600 are also accepted. - Grammar. A value is an arithmetic expression with + − × / (also typed *), parentheses and unit-suffixed terms (mm, cm, m, ', ", fractions such as 3 1/2"). Unsuffixed numbers use the project's length unit. The same parser is used by every numeric field in the Properties palette (UI chapter). - Errors. An unparsable entry turns the box red and is not committed ("Invalid value"). Zero or negative lengths are rejected ("Value must be greater than 0"). A length shorter than TOL_SHORT gives "Element is too short". The box stays open so the user can correct it. - Listening dimensions are not available for splines or rectangles, because those inputs have more than one dimension. - Replay.
