    Commands. roof.join(roof_id, edge_ref, target_ref) and roof.unjoin(roof_id, edge_ref?).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A dormer roof joined to the main roof ends exactly on the main roof's top surface, with no gap or overlap greater than TOL_POINT.

    3.6.10 Shape editing (floors, roofs, structural floors, toposolids)

    ID: ARC-SHAPE-001 · Priority: P1 · Ref: research/02 §1, §7.5, §17.7 · screenshots/architecture/shape_editing_points_toposolid.png

    Purpose. Warp the top surface of a slab with points and split lines, for falls to drains, terrain and similar cases.

    UI. With an element selected, the Shape Editing panel offers:

    Tool Behaviour
    Modify Sub Elements Select points or edges (Tab cycles between them). A blue arrow drags vertically, and a red square (toposolids only) drags horizontally. A text control or the Elevation field sets the exact height relative to the Elevation Base (Current Level, Project Base Point, Survey Point or Internal Origin). Dragging an edge moves its middle and keeps the relative heights of its ends
    Add Point Along Surface mode (with Offset from Surface) or Absolute mode (with Elevation)
    Add Split Line From a vertex, edge, face or point to another. Uses the same two modes, and snaps with temporary dimensions
    Pick Supports Creates split lines along picked beams and lowers the slab bottom onto them (structural floors)
    Convert folding lines to split lines Turns automatic triangulation edges into explicit split lines
    Reset Shape Removes every modifier
    Snap to Editor Points and Lines Toggle, off by default
    Snap XYZ Reports the Z of the reference object
    Preview Points Toggles the display of points, for performance
    Copy/Paste Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V of points and lines inside edit mode, including between toposolids

    Behaviour & rules. 1. Modifier set. The modifier set is: - the boundary vertices, each with a height offset (default 0); - added points (x, y, z_offset); - split lines (polylines with heights at their vertices; between vertices, heights interpolate linearly along the line). 2. Triangulation. A constrained Delaunay triangulation (CDT) is built in plan, with: - vertices: boundary vertices, added points and split-line vertices; - constraints: boundary edges, hole edges and split-line segments.

    Arcs in the boundary are first discretised to a chord error of 1 mm. The triangulation uses the spade crate (MIT/Apache-2.0), or an equivalent library with a compatible licence. 3. Folding lines are the triangulation edges that are not constraints. Folding lines are hidden by default. 4. Top surface. Each triangle is lifted to the heights of its vertices, giving planar facets. A point added Along Surface takes the current height of the surface at its (x, y) position plus its offset, evaluated once, at insertion. After that its height is absolute. 5. Layers. The behaviour depends on the type: - No variable layer: the whole slab follows the warped top with constant thickness. Each layer surface is the top surface offset along the facet normals (floors and roofs, BRepOffsetAPI_MakeOffsetShape with intersection joins) or straight down (toposolids). - One variable layer: the layers above the variable layer follow the warped top. The layers below it keep the original flat (or sloped-plane) shape. The variable layer fills the space between, and it must stay ≥ 0 thick everywhere; otherwise Reviera reports "Variable layer would be negative" and does not commit the edit. 6. Curved Edge Condition (instance, for arc boundaries): Conform to curve keeps the arc edge on the surface; Project to side uses vertical faces on the arc. 7. Validation. Points outside the boundary are rejected. A split line that crosses another split line creates a vertex where they cross, whose height is interpolated from the first line.

    Regeneration. Shape modifiers belong to the host. Changing the boundary keeps points that are still inside and discards the others, with a warning.

    Data (IFC mapping). - The modifiers are stored in RXD element data: sketch (role shape) for floors and roofs, and recipe.toposolid for toposolids. - The body becomes an IfcFacetedBrep (IFC4) or an IfcPolygonalFaceSet with Closed = TRUE. - IfcMaterialLayerSetUsage is kept. For a variable layer, IFC4 offers IfcMaterialLayerWithOffsets, which cannot describe a free-form variable thickness. Reviera writes the nominal thickness and puts the true geometry in the body.

    Commands. - shape.add_point(element_id, xy, mode: AlongSurface(offset)|Absolute(z), elevation_base?) -> key - shape.add_split_line(element_id, points: [xy], mode, heights?) -> key - shape.move(element_id, keys, dz?, dxy?) - shape.set_elevation(element_id, keys, z, elevation_base?) - shape.pick_supports(element_id, beam_ids) - shape.convert_folding_lines(element_id) - shape.reset(element_id) - shape.copy(element_id, keys) -> clip (query) - shape.paste(element_id, clip, offset?)

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A flat roof with one point dropped 50 mm in the middle of a 10 m × 10 m area, with an insulation layer marked variable, gives four planar facets falling to the drain. The deck stays flat, and the insulation thickness at the drain is reduced by exactly 50 mm. - [ ] Without a variable layer, the same edit lowers the whole slab, and the thickness measured perpendicular to each facet stays constant. - [ ] Reset Shape restores the original body exactly, and the body's hash matches the one recorded before the edit.

    3.6.11 Parts: model and creation

    ID: ARC-PART-001 · Priority: P2 · Ref: research/02 §2.1 (Figure 1, Create panel), §4.5 · web: About Parts; Create Parts

    Purpose. Break design elements into the pieces that will actually be built (each layer of a wall, each slab layer, pieces of a layer divided into panels), so that construction modellers can schedule, tag, filter, sequence and export them, while the design element stays the single source of geometry.

    Workflow. 1. The user selects eligible elements and chooses Modify | <Element> › Create › Create Parts, or starts Modify › Create › Create Parts first, picks elements (ineligible ones are drawn in half-tone and cannot be picked) and presses Enter or Spacebar. 2. Reviera creates the parts in one transaction. The current view switches its Parts Visibility to Show Parts if it was Show Original, and the status bar reports how many parts were created. 3. The user selects parts to divide (ARC-PART-002), merge or exclude (ARC-PART-003), or to edit their properties (ARC-PART-004).

    Behaviour & rules. - Eligible sources. Elements with a compound structure: basic walls (not stacked or curtain walls, and not wall sweeps), foundation walls, floors and structural floors (except shape-edited floors with more than one layer), roofs by footprint, extrusion or face, ceilings, foundation slabs, slab edges, fascias and gutters. Family instances of the categories structural framing, columns and structural columns are also eligible, and give a single part each. Elements in a linked model are eligible; their parts live in the host model. An element that already has parts is not eligible again. - One part per layer. A layered source gives one part per non-membrane layer (membranes, which have zero thickness, give none). A vertically compound wall (ARC-CMPD-003) gives one part per region. Each part's solid is the layer's solid after joins, layer cleanup, wrapping, attachment, extensions and insert voids, so the parts tile the source exactly with no gaps or overlaps. - Identity. A part is identified by (source GlobalId, layer or region sub-reference, division path), where the division path lists the divisions and pieces that led to it. The identity is stable across regeneration, so a part keeps its GlobalId, Mark and overrides while its source changes, as long as the same layer and piece still exist. - Source changes. Parts regenerate automatically whenever the source changes, after the source's body stage: - geometry, joins, openings, inserts, orientation (flip) or thickness: every part is rebuilt and its divisions re-applied; - type change or layers added or removed: parts are matched to the new layers by layer sub-reference, then by function and order. A new layer gets a new, undivided part; a part whose layer has gone is deleted, together with its descendants, and the deletion is listed in a warning; - material change of a layer: parts with Material By Original on follow it; - the source becomes ineligible (for example a floor is shape-edited and has several layers): its parts keep their last geometry and are flagged "Source cannot be divided into parts". - Delete and copy. Deleting the source deletes all its parts and their descendants (after a confirmation that gives the count). Copying, mirroring or arraying the source copies its parts, divisions, merges, exclusions and overrides. A source whose parts exist is still editable in every way. - Linked sources. When the link is unloaded or the source element disappears from it, the parts keep their last geometry and are flagged "Source unavailable"; they regenerate when the link is reloaded. - Selection. In a view showing parts, clicking selects a part; the source element is not selectable there (ARC-PART-004). Tab cycles between overlapping parts.

    Regeneration. A host edge from the source element's body stage to each part (inserts reach the parts through the source's cut body, so they need no edge of their own), and datum edges from the references used by divisions (ARC-PART-002). Parts of one source regenerate together; different sources regenerate in parallel.

    Data (IFC mapping). - Each part that currently exists as a leaf (not divided further, not absorbed in a merge) is an IfcBuildingElementPart that decomposes its source element through IfcRelAggregates (RelatingObject = source, RelatedObjects = its parts). PredefinedType = INSULATION for parts of Thermal/Air layers, PRECASTPANEL for parts the STR chapter marks as precast, otherwise USERDEFINED with ObjectType = the layer function (for example "Finish 1"), or NOTDEFINED for single-part family sources. - Each part has its own Body (an IfcExtrudedAreaSolid where the piece is prismatic, otherwise an IfcFacetedBrep) and its own IfcRelAssociatesMaterial with an IfcMaterial. It is contained in the storey of its Base Level (or the source's storey when Non Associated). - Source body. By default (export option Parts: replace source body, on), a source that has parts is written with its Axis/FootPrint representation and its material layer set but without a Body, so that tools which read both do not count the volume twice. With the option off, both bodies are written. - Excluded parts (ARC-PART-003) are not exported. Intermediate parts (divided or merged away) are not exported; their history is kept in RXD. - RXD element data (recipe.part) on each part holds its identity tuple, its parent part, its division and merge membership, its excluded flag and its overrides. Division and merge definitions are project-level and stored in RXD document model/parts. - Import. An IfcBuildingElementPart without RXD data is imported as a non-parametric part of its aggregating element; it cannot be divided further until the user regenerates parts from the source (parts.create on the source replaces it after confirmation).

    Commands. parts.create(host_ids) -> [element_id] returns the new parts. Ineligible elements in host_ids are skipped and listed in the result warning; if none is eligible the command fails with "No element can be divided into parts".

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Create Parts on a wall with brick, cavity insulation, block and plaster layers and a window creates four parts whose volumes add up to the wall's volume within 0.01%, each with the opening cut. - [ ] Changing the wall's block thickness from 100 to 140 mm regenerates the parts in place; their GlobalIds and Marks are unchanged. - [ ] Changing the wall to a type without the plaster layer deletes the plaster part and reports it. - [ ] The IFC export contains one IfcBuildingElementPart per part, aggregated by the IfcWall, and the IfcWall has no Body representation; IfcOpenShell's validator reports no errors. - [ ] A stacked wall and a curtain wall cannot be picked while Create Parts is active.

    3.6.12 Dividing parts

    ID: ARC-PART-002 · Priority: P2 · Ref: research/02 §2.3 · web: Divide Parts; Edit a Part Division; Division Instance Properties; Create a Division Profile Family

    Purpose. Cut parts into smaller pieces (panels, pours, sheets) along sketched lines or along levels, grids and reference planes, optionally with a gap and a profiled edge.

    Workflow. 1. The user selects one or more parts and chooses Modify | Parts › Part › Divide Parts. A division session opens: the selected parts are tinted, an outline offset 300 mm (at view scale) outside their combined extent is drawn dashed, and the Division properties appear in the Properties palette. 2. By sketch: the user chooses Edit Sketch, sets or shows the work plane (Work Plane panel; default: the plane of the largest face of the first part), sketches division curves and chooses Finish Sketch. 3. By references: the user chooses Intersecting References. The dialog lists the levels, grids and named reference planes that intersect the parts, with a filter drop-down (All, Levels, Grids, Reference Planes) and an Offset column per reference (positive or negative, default 0). The user ticks references and presses OK. 4. The user sets Divider Gap and the profile options (below) and can Add or Remove parts from the division. 5. Finish Edit Mode applies the division; Cancel discards the session. 6. Later, selecting any part made by a division and choosing Edit Division reopens the same session: the original parts are shown in a light tint and the division curves in a highlight colour; curves can be dragged, deleted or added, references changed, and parts added or removed.

    Behaviour & rules. - Division curves. Lines, arcs, splines and closed loops on one work plane. An open chain must cross the parts' dashed outline at both ends (it is extended to infinity in its end directions for the cut); a closed loop cuts out an island. Curves that do not cross any part are kept but have no effect, and the session warns about them on Finish. - Cut. Each curve is swept along the work-plane normal into a cutting surface that passes right through the parts (BRepPrimAPI_MakePrism of the curve over the parts' extent plus 1 m each way). References are used as infinite planes moved by their offset. All cutting surfaces split each part in one BRepAlgoAPI_Splitter call; every resulting solid becomes a new part, and the parent part stays in the model as a hidden intermediate element. - Divider Gap (≥ 0, default 0) removes a slab of that width centred on each cutting surface (BRepAlgoAPI_Cut with the surface thickened by ±gap/2 using BRepOffsetAPI_MakeThickSolid). A piece that disappears entirely within a gap is not created, and the session reports it. - Edge profile. Split Profile Type (default None) applies a division profile (a 2D profile family whose usage is Generic; DM chapter) along each divider edge. Edge Match decides how the two faces of a joint are shaped: Complementary (one side gets the profile as a tongue, the other the matching groove), Mirrored (both sides get the profile mirrored across the divider) or Rotated (the second side gets the profile turned 180° about the divider line). Profile Along Flip swaps which side gets which shape (all three modes); Profile Across Flip turns the profile over across the part thickness (Complementary and Rotated only). Profile Offset moves the profile from the divider centre. The profile is swept along the divider edge on each piece and added or subtracted (BRepOffsetAPI_MakePipeShell, then fuse or cut). - Nesting. A part made by a division can itself be divided; the division path grows by one level. Editing an outer division re-runs the inner ones on the new pieces; an inner division whose curves no longer cross its part leaves the part whole. - Following references. Divisions by reference follow their references: moving a grid moves the cut. A sketched division has a datum edge to its work plane's host. - Adding and removing parts in a session (or with the commands) only changes which parts the same curves and references cut. Removing a part restores it as one piece and deletes its descendants after a warning. - Session recovery. The division session is an interactive tool (conventions §2.1). Its micro-operation schema is: begin {part_ids | division_id}, the sketch.* operations, set_refs {[(ref, offset)]}, set_props {gap, profile}, add_parts {ids}, remove_parts {ids}, finish, cancel. Replaying them on the model state at begin rebuilds the session after a crash.

    Data (IFC mapping). The division definition (parts, curves with work plane, references with offsets, gap and profile settings) is stored in RXD document model/parts (kind part.division) under a division ID. Only the resulting leaf parts are exported (ARC-PART-001); the gap is visible as the space between them.

    Commands. - parts.divide(part_ids, curves?: [curve], work_plane?: plane | host_ref, refs?: [{ref, offset}], gap?: f64, profile?: {type_id, edge_match: Complementary|Mirrored|Rotated, flip_along?: bool, flip_across?: bool, offset?: f64}) -> {division_id, parts: [element_id]} divides non-interactively. - parts.division_begin(part_ids | division_id) -> session_id opens the interactive session; within it, the sketch.* commands edit curves. - parts.division_set(session_id, refs?, gap?, profile?), parts.division_add(session_id, part_ids) and parts.division_remove(session_id, part_ids) change it. - parts.division_finish(session_id) -> {division_id, parts: [element_id]} and parts.division_cancel(session_id) end it.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Dividing a 10 m brick part with three vertical sketch lines 2.5 m apart and a 10 mm gap gives four pieces whose lengths are 2.495, 2.49, 2.49 and 2.495 m. - [ ] Dividing the parts of a 4-storey wall by the intersecting levels with offset +50 mm gives one piece per storey; raising Level 3 by 300 mm moves that cut by 300 mm. - [ ] A Complementary tongue-and-groove profile gives matching faces: the two pieces fused together have the same volume as the undivided part minus the gap volume, within 0.01%. - [ ] Killing the process during a division session and reopening the file offers to restore the session, and restoring it reproduces the sketched curves exactly.

    3.6.13 Merging, excluding, restoring and deleting parts

    ID: ARC-PART-003 · Priority: P2 · Ref: research/02 §2.1 · web: Work with Merged Parts; Exclude Parts; Delete a Part

    Purpose. Join pieces that will be built as one, take pieces out of the quantities without deleting them, and undo part creation.

    Workflow. - Merge: select two or more parts › Modify | Parts › Part › Merge Parts. To change a merge, select the merged part › Edit Merged, then Add or Remove parts and Finish. Edit Merged is also offered inside an Edit Division session when the division contains a merged part; the edit modes nest as deep as needed. - Exclude: select parts › Modify | Parts › Exclude › Exclude Parts. Restore: hover an excluded part (it highlights), click it, and choose Restore Parts or click the Restore excluded part control shown next to it. - Delete: select a part and press Delete. A warning says that the edit deletes parts and lists how many; Delete Element(s) confirms.

    Behaviour & rules. - Merge conditions. All parts must have the same material (after overrides) and must touch or overlap: every part must share a face area of at least 1 mm² or a common volume with another part in the set (connectivity over the whole set). Parts of different source elements may be merged. Failures: fewer than two parts ("Select at least two parts"), different materials ("Parts with different materials cannot be merged"), or not connected ("Merged part would have disconnected pieces"). - Merge geometry. BRepAlgoAPI_Fuse of the parts, then ShapeUpgrade_UnifySameDomain to remove internal faces. The merged part takes the first picked part's Mark, comments and overrides; the merged-away parts become hidden intermediates. - Later changes. If a source change makes a merged part disconnected, the merge is kept as a multi-body part and a warning names it; the user can remove pieces from the merge. Removing parts until fewer than two remain dissolves the merge. - Edit Merged recovery. The Edit Merged mode is an interactive tool (conventions §2.1) with the micro-operations begin {merged_part_id}, add {ids}, remove {ids}, finish and cancel; replaying them rebuilds an interrupted session. - Exclude. An excluded part stays in the model but is not drawn (except when highlighted under the cursor or selected), is left out of schedules, material take-offs, area and volume totals, clash detection and IFC export, and does not cut or join. Dimensions to it are kept. Excluding a merged part excludes it as a whole. Restore reverses all of this. - Delete. Deleting a part also deletes every part derived from it (its division descendants and any merge that contains it). Deleting one piece of a division deletes the whole division result (all its sibling pieces, listed in the warning) and reveals the parent part again. Deleting a first-level part deletes all parts of that source and reveals the source element; this is how Create Parts is undone later.

    Data (IFC mapping). Merge definitions are stored in RXD document model/parts (kind part.merge); the excluded flag is in each part's RXD element data (recipe.part). A merged part is exported as one IfcBuildingElementPart. Excluded parts are not exported.

    Commands. - parts.merge(part_ids) -> element_id - parts.edit_merged(merged_part_id, add?: [element_id], remove?: [element_id]) - parts.exclude(part_ids) and parts.restore(part_ids) - element.delete(element_ids[], confirm_dependents?=true) -> element_ids[] (ARC-MOD-014) deletes parts and returns the descendants deleted with them.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Merging three adjacent plasterboard pieces gives one part whose volume is their sum and which has no internal faces. - [ ] Merging a brick piece with a block piece is refused with the material message. - [ ] An excluded part does not appear in a part schedule or in the IFC export, and Restore brings it back with the same GlobalId. - [ ] Deleting one of four pieces of a divided brick part deletes all four pieces and shows the undivided brick part again; deleting that part then removes every part of the wall and shows the wall.

    3.6.14 Part properties, visibility and scheduling

    ID: ARC-PART-004 · Priority: P2 · Ref: research/02 §2.2 · web: Part Instance Properties; Control Part Visibility and Appearance

    Purpose. Give each part its own construction data (material, level, phasing, identity) and control in each view whether parts, their source elements or both are shown.

    UI. - View property Parts Visibility (Graphics group): Show Parts (default for new views; parts are drawn and selectable, sources are hidden and not selectable), Show Original (sources are drawn and selectable, parts hidden; the source cannot be picked by Create Parts in this mode), Show Both (both drawn and separately selectable). View templates can control it. - Object style. Parts is a top-level model category with its own cut and projection line weights, colour, pattern and material, and can be overridden per view or per element (DOC chapter). Its cut pattern is the part's material cut pattern. - Shape handles. With Show Shape Handles on, a selected part shows a handle on each planar face; dragging one moves that face along its normal (Edit Part Geometry). The offset is stored per face sub-reference.

    Behaviour & rules. - Instance parameters: - Base Level (default: the source's level; another level or Non Associated); - Volume, Area (the largest face), Height, and, for parts of walls, Length and Width (all read-only, from the part's solid); - Comments, Mark; - Show Shape Handles; - Original Category, Original Family, Original Type (read-only, from the source); - Material By Original (bool, default on) and Material (editable only when Material By Original is off); - Construction = Core or Finish (read-only: Core for layers between the core boundaries, Finish otherwise); - Phase Created By Original and Phase Demolished By Original (bool, default on) and Phase Created and Phase Demolished (editable only when the matching flag is off). - Overrides persist. Material, phase and level overrides, Mark and Comments are kept through source regeneration as long as the part's identity exists (ARC-PART-001). Divided pieces inherit their parent's overrides; a merged part takes those of its first part. - Face offsets (shape handles) are re-applied after each regeneration; an offset that would make the part invalid (zero or negative thickness) is clamped and reported. - Scheduling. Parts can be scheduled and tagged like any category, with the parameters above. Excluded parts, hidden intermediates and merged-away parts never appear; a merged part appears once. Material take-offs use the part's material and volume. - Rebar. Concrete parts can host reinforcement and carry rebar cover (STR chapter); precast splitting (STR chapter) uses this parts engine.

    Data (IFC mapping). Parameters are written as property values on the IfcBuildingElementPart; Base Level gives its storey containment; the phase values follow the phasing rules (DOC chapter). Volume, Area, Length, Width and Height are written as an IfcElementQuantity named "BaseQuantities". Overrides and face offsets are stored in RXD element data (recipe.part). Parts Visibility is view data (RXD document views/<viewId>).

    Commands. - parts.set_overrides(part_ids, material?: ByOriginal | material_id, base_level?: ByOriginal | level_id | NonAssociated, phase_created?: ByOriginal | phase_id, phase_demolished?: ByOriginal | phase_id | None) - parts.offset_face(part_id, face_ref, distance) - view.set_parts_visibility(view_id, mode: ShowParts|ShowOriginal|ShowBoth) -> () - element.set_param for Mark, Comments and other writable parameters.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Turning Material By Original off on one plaster part and choosing lime render changes only that part; changing the wall type's plaster material afterwards changes the other plaster parts but not that one. - [ ] A view set to Show Original shows and selects the wall, not its parts; Show Both lets each be selected separately. - [ ] A part schedule grouped by Original Type and Construction lists core and finish parts separately and omits excluded parts. - [ ] Dragging a part's top face up 50 mm with its shape handle survives a later change of the wall's height (the face stays 50 mm above the new top).

    3.7 Stairs, railings and ramps

    3.7.1 Stair assembly model

    ID: ARC-STAIR-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.1, §17.8 · screenshots/architecture/stair_t_shaped_component_assembly.png

    Purpose. A stair is an assembly of related components that is edited in a dedicated assembly mode.

    Behaviour & rules. - Components: - Runs: straight, full-step spiral, centre-ends spiral, L-shaped winder, U-shaped winder or sketched; - Landings: automatic, picked from two runs, or sketched; - Supports: stringers and carriages, created automatically from the type or by Pick Edges; - Railings: generated on Finish. - Relationship graph (inside the stair recipe): - Each run knows its relative_base_height and relative_top_height within the stair. - Runs that are connected through a landing share that landing's height. - When the user removes risers from one run, the next connected run gains the same number, so the total riser count stays equal to N_desired. Reviera applies this rebalancing to the downstream run along the stair path, or to the upstream run if no downstream run exists. - Automatic and picked landings reshape when their runs move. Sketched landings do not. - Arrangements. Overlapping and T-shaped arrangements (several runs meeting one landing) are allowed. - A stair cannot be a member of an assembly element. - Single editing path. There is no separate legacy "stair by sketch" tool. Sketching happens through Create Sketch inside the assembly.

    Data (IFC mapping). - IfcStair with an IfcStairType aggregates (IfcRelAggregates): - IfcStairFlight per run (PredefinedType = STRAIGHT, WINDER, SPIRAL, CURVED or FREEFORM), with NumberOfRisers, NumberOfTreads, RiserHeight and TreadLength set (IFC4 occurrence attributes) and Pset_StairFlightCommon; - IfcSlab with PredefinedType = LANDING per landing; - IfcMember with PredefinedType = STRINGER per support (carriages are USERDEFINED, ObjectType "CARRIAGE"); - IfcRailing per generated railing. - IfcStair.PredefinedType is classified from the arrangement: one straight run → STRAIGHT_RUN_STAIR; two straight runs in line → TWO_STRAIGHT_RUN_STAIR; an L shape with a landing → QUARTER_TURN_STAIR; an L winder → QUARTER_WINDING_STAIR; a U shape with a landing → HALF_TURN_STAIR; a U winder → HALF_WINDING_STAIR; a spiral → SPIRAL_STAIR; a curved run → CURVED_RUN_STAIR; two runs meeting one landing from opposite sides → DOUBLE_RETURN_STAIR; otherwise USERDEFINED. - Pset_StairCommon holds NumberOfRiser, NumberOfTreads, RiserHeight, TreadLength, RequiredHeadroom where it is set, and IsExternal. - The full recipe is stored in RXD element data (recipe.stair).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A U-shaped stair (two runs and a landing) exports IfcStair(HALF_TURN_STAIR) aggregating two IfcStairFlight, one IfcSlab(LANDING), its supports and its railings.

    3.7.2 Creating stairs by component

    ID: ARC-STAIR-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.2 · screenshots/architecture/stair_direct_manipulation_controls.png

    Workflow. 1. The user starts Architecture › Circulation › Stair in a plan or 3D view. Tiling a plan view and a 3D view side by side is recommended. 2. In the Components panel, Run is selected. The Draw gallery offers Straight, Full-Step Spiral, Center-Ends Spiral, L-Shape Winder, U-Shape Winder and Create Sketch. 3. The user sets the options: - Location Line: Exterior Support: Left, Run: Left, Run: Center, Run: Right or Exterior Support: Right, relative to the up direction; - Offset: positive to the right of the path; - Actual Run Width: the width without supports; - Automatic Landing: on by default. 4. The user picks the stair type (Assembled, Cast-in-Place or Precast) and sets the New Stairs and New Stairs: Runs properties. 5. Tools › Railing: the user chooses a railing type or None, and a position of Treads or Stringer. 6. The user draws runs: - Straight: click a start point. The tooltip shows how many risers have been created and how many remain. Click an end point. To make a landing, click when the run has the risers wanted, then click further along the extension line to start the next run. The landing depth defaults to the run width. - Full-Step Spiral: click the centre, then the radius. Every remaining riser is placed counter-clockwise; the stair may exceed 360°; Flip reverses the direction. - Center-Ends Spiral: click the centre, the start and the end (less than 360°). - L or U winder: one click places the whole winder. Mirror Preview and Spacebar change the turn. The winder snaps to walls. Direct-manipulation controls balance the legs, and Parallel Treads at Start/End replace winder treads with parallel ones. 7. Landings: Pick Two Runs (two runs in the same session whose end and start heights match) or Create Sketch. 8. Supports: Pick Edges (Tab picks a continuous boundary, with mitered joins). The stair type must have a side support type. 9. Finish Edit Mode generates the railings.

    UI. - Other assembly-mode tools: Flip (reverses the up direction), Convert (turns a component into a sketched component; one-way, after a confirmation), Edit Sketch, Connect Levels (multistory; Align with Mid-Landing or Run-Start) and Railing. - Direct-manipulation controls in plan: - run-end arrows: drag to add or remove risers; the next run is rebalanced; - run-width arrows on both sides; - riser-count controls at both ends; - winder leg-balance dots; - spiral radius and angle handles; - landing edge arrows (automatic landings).

    Commands. - stair.create(type_id, base_level, top_level | Unconnected(height), base_offset?, top_offset?, desired_risers?, tread_depth?, runs: [RunSpec], landings?: [LandingSpec], supports?: [SupportSpec], railing?: {type_id | None, position: Treads|Stringer}) -> element_id - RunSpec = {kind: Straight{start,end} | FullSpiral{center,radius,start_angle,ccw} | CenterEndsSpiral{center,start,end} | LWinder{corner, leg1, leg2, mirror} | UWinder{...} | Sketch{left: [curve], right: [curve], risers: [curve], path?: [curve]}, location_line, offset, width, begin_with_riser, end_with_riser, risers?} - LandingSpec = Auto | PickRuns(a,b) | Sketch{loops, path?} - stair.edit(stair_id) -> session_id (opens an assembly session) - stair.add_run(session_id, RunSpec) -> key - stair.add_landing(session_id, LandingSpec) -> key - stair.add_support(session_id, edge_refs, side) -> key - stair.set_run_risers(session_id, run_key, n) - stair.flip(session_id) - stair.convert_to_sketch(session_id, component_key) - stair.finish(session_id) - stair.cancel(session_id)

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A straight stair from Level 1 (0.0) to Level 2 (3.0) with Maximum Riser 0.18 creates 17 risers of 0.17647 m, and the tooltip counts down to 0. - [ ] Clicking after 9 risers, then continuing in line, gives a landing whose depth equals the run width, and a second run of 8 risers. - [ ] Dragging the end arrow of run 1 to remove 2 risers adds 2 risers to run 2, and the total height is unchanged.

    3.7.3 Stair calculation rules

    ID: ARC-STAIR-003 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.4

    Behaviour & rules. - Inputs: - H = z_top − z_base, where z_top is the top level plus its offset (or the Desired Stair Height when the top is unconnected); - the type's Maximum Riser Height R_max, Minimum Tread Depth T_min and Minimum Run Width W_min; - the instance's Desired Number of Risers N_d and Actual Tread Depth T. - Derivation: 1. N_min = ceil(H / R_max − 1e-9). The default N_d is N_min. If the user enters N_d < N_min, Reviera warns "Riser height exceeds maximum", and the value is allowed but flagged. 2. Actual riser height R = H / N_d. 3. Treads per run. For a run with k risers, Begin with Riser B and End with Riser E: treads = k − 1 + (1 − B) + (1 − E). Each flag that is off adds a tread at that end, while the riser count stays the same. 4. Straight run length = treads · T. 5. Winder treads. The user's tread depth T is applied at the walking line, which lies at the path offset (by default the run's centre line). Inner and outer tread widths follow the winder geometry (ARC-STAIR-004). 6. Spiral runs. The angle per tread is φ = T / r_w, where r_w is the walking-line radius. Total angle = treads · φ. - Stair Calculator (optional, on the type): the rule a ≤ m·R + n·T ≤ b, with user-set m, n, a and b. The default is m = 2, n = 1, a = 0.60 m and b = 0.65 m. If the rule is not met, Reviera shows a warning, not an error. - Validation warnings: R > R_max, T < T_min, run width < W_min, and "Not enough risers placed" when a run session is finished with risers remaining. In that last case the stair is still created, and its top is not connected. - Multistory stairs. Connect Levels (or Multistory Top Level) repeats the stair between each pair of consecutive selected levels. The repetitions are generated copies. If the story heights differ, each copy recomputes N and R for its own story while keeping the same run layout. A copy whose layout cannot fit gets its own warning.

    Commands. stair.set_rules(type_id, max_riser, min_tread, min_width, calculator?: {m,n,min,max}) and stair.connect_levels(stair_id, level_ids, align_with: MidLanding|RunStart).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] With H = 2.8 m, R_max = 0.19 and B = E = true, the stair has 15 risers of 0.18667 m and 14 treads. - [ ] Turning End with Riser off adds one tread and leaves the riser count at 15. - [ ] A multistory stair connecting levels with story heights of 3.0 m and 3.3 m has 17 risers in the first copy and 19 in the second, with R_max = 0.18.

    3.7.4 Stair geometry generation

    ID: ARC-STAIR-004 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.2–§8.4, §17.8

    Behaviour & rules. Each component is generated independently (in parallel), using its own frame: s along the path, w across the width and z up. 1. Straight monolithic run (cast-in-place): - Build the side profile in the (s, z) plane: - a step polyline: riser R (vertical, or slanted by the Slanted riser setting) and tread T + nosing length ν (each tread overhangs the riser below by ν); - the underside: for Smooth, a line parallel to the pitch line (through the tread nosings) at a perpendicular distance of Structural Depth; for Stepped, a copy of the steps offset downward by the structural depth. - Close the profile at the bottom with a horizontal line to the floor and at the top with a vertical line. - Extrude it across the width (BRepPrimAPI_MakePrism). - The nosing profile (if any) is swept along the front edge of each tread and fused. 2. Straight non-monolithic run (assembled): - each tread is a prism of the tread profile (a rectangle T + ν by tread thickness, or a tread-profile family); - each riser is a plate between consecutive treads; - Apply Nosing Profile (Front only, Front and Left, Front and Right, or Front, Left and Right) sweeps the nosing profile along the matching tread edges. 3. Winder runs: - The walking line γ is the path at the walking offset. - Tread boundaries are placed every T along γ. - Inside the turn, each boundary is a line through its point on γ, at an angle that varies linearly from parallel (at the ends of the parallel-tread zones) to radial through the inner corner point (at the turn's middle). This "balanced" distribution gives a positive inner tread width wherever the minimum inner width (1/3 of T, configurable) allows. - If the minimum inner width cannot be met, Reviera warns "Winder inner width below minimum". - Each tread is the polygon between consecutive boundaries and the run's side lines, extruded by the tread thickness at height i·R. 4. Spiral runs. Each tread is an annular sector [r_in, r_out] × [θ_i, θ_i + φ], built with BRepPrimAPI_MakeRevol of a rectangle about the centre axis or as a prism of the sector face, at height i·R. A monolithic underside is a helicoidal ruled surface between the inner and outer helices offset downward by the structural depth. It is built with BRepOffsetAPI_ThruSections through radial section lines every 5°. 5. Landings. - An automatic landing between two runs is the convex hull of the end edge of the incoming run and the start edge of the outgoing run, extended so that its depth along each run equals at least the run width. - A landing between collinear runs is a rectangle (width × run width). - Its top is at the shared height, and its thickness comes from the landing type (Monolithic, or Use Same Tread/Riser Settings as Run). - The solid is a prism of the outline (BRepPrimAPI_MakePrism, downward). - A sketched landing uses its sketch loop. 6. Supports: - Stringer (closed): a plate in the (s, z) plane, between lines parallel to the pitch line at the support's top and bottom offsets. It is trimmed horizontally at the floor and the top level (BRepAlgoAPI_Cut with half-spaces) and positioned at the side with the lateral offset. On winders and spirals, the support is swept along the side curve (BRepOffsetAPI_MakePipeShell) and lifted along a helical law. - Carriage (open): a profile placed under the treads, either sawtooth or straight. - Middle supports: n carriages spaced evenly across the width. - Picked supports: the profile is swept along the picked edge chain, with miter joins. 7. Cut by levels. Every component is cut by the half-space below z_base − 1 mm, so that nothing hangs below the base floor. 8. Plan representation (DOC chapter): the cut line and the parts above the cut are drawn dashed, by subcategory. The stair path, up/down text and tread and riser numbers are annotation.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A cast-in-place straight run with structural depth 150 mm has an underside parallel to the pitch line, at a perpendicular distance of 150 mm from the nosing line. - [ ] An L winder with three winder treads has walking-line tread depths equal to T within 0.1 mm, and every inner tread width is greater than 0. - [ ] The volume of a full-step spiral with 16 treads matches the analytic sector volume within 0.5%.

    3.7.5 Stair parameters

    ID: ARC-STAIR-005 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.3, §8.4

    Level Parameters
    Stair type Calculation Rules (Maximum Riser Height, Minimum Tread Depth, Minimum Run Width, Calculator); Construction (Run Type, Landing Type, Function); End Connection (precast: Straight Cut or Notch, with notch dimensions); Supports (Right/Left Support = None, Stringer (Closed) or Carriage (Open); Right/Left Support Type; Right/Left Lateral Offset; Middle Support, its type and count); identity data
    Stair instance Base Level, Base Offset, Top Level (default: the next level, or Unconnected), Top Offset, Desired Stair Height, Multistory Top Level and connected levels, Desired Number of Risers, Actual Number of Risers (RO), Actual Riser Height (RO), Actual Tread Depth, Tread/Riser Start Number, phasing
    Run type (Monolithic or Non-Monolithic) Underside Surface (Smooth or Stepped), Structural Depth, Monolithic/Tread/Riser Material, Tread (on/off, thickness, profile, Nosing Length, nosing profile, Apply Nosing Profile), Riser (on/off, Slanted, thickness, profile, Riser to Tread Connection)
    Run instance Location Path Justification, Relative Base Height, Relative Top Height, Run Height, Actual Run Width, Begin with Riser, End with Riser, Actual Number of Risers and Treads, Actual Riser Height, Actual Tread Depth, Parallel Treads at Start/End (winders)
    Landing type Monolithic or Non-monolithic, Thickness, Material, Use Same Tread/Riser Settings as Run

    Sketched components. Run › Create Sketch takes Boundary curves (left and right, which must not touch; each may have several segments), Riser curves, and an optional Stair Path. A sketched run has no automatic relationships. A monolithic stair with zero tread thickness is allowed.

    Data (IFC mapping). The run type and landing type are IfcStairFlightType and IfcSlabType (LANDING), and their recipes are stored in RXD type data (recipe.stair_type).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A sketched run with a curved left boundary and a straight right boundary generates treads between its riser curves, and keeps them when the stair width parameter changes.

    3.7.6 Stair annotation

    ID: ARC-STAIR-006 · Priority: P1 · Ref: research/02 §1 (2027), §8.4

    Behaviour & rules. - Stair path (Stair Path type: up and down arrows, start and end symbols). - Cut mark (single or double zig-zag, set by type). - Up/down text. - Tread/riser numbering (the Number Tread/Riser tool). The numbers have type properties: font, size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, background, and independent display above and below the cut line. They have their own visibility categories and work with Tag All Not Tagged. - Rule-Based Numbering (Manage › Numbering) is specified in Chapter 2 §2.10.16 (DM-NUM-001). - The editing colour used in assembly mode can be configured.

    These are view annotation and are specified in the DOC chapter. This chapter requires that the stair recipe expose, for each tread and riser, a stable key, its nosing line, its centre point and its number.

    Commands. stair.number_treads(view_id, stair_id, start_number?, type_id?) -> element_id.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Tread numbers keep their values after a run is moved. They change only when the number of treads changes.

    3.7.7 Railings

    ID: ARC-RAIL-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.5, §17.9

    Purpose. Railing systems, either free-standing or hosted on stairs, ramps, floors, slab edges, wall tops, roofs or toposolids.

    Workflow. - Sketch Path. The user starts Architecture › Circulation › Railing › Sketch Path. 1. Optionally, the user uses Pick New Host; otherwise the railing starts on the current level. 2. The user sketches one connected chain, open or closed. On stairs, the chain is sketched along the inside of the stringer. 3. Canvas controls: Toggle Sketch Orientation (swaps start and end) and, for closed loops, Move Beginning to Next Corner. 4. Finish. - Place on Stair/Ramp. The user picks a stair or ramp, and the railing is hosted on the Treads or the Stringer. - Railings are also created automatically with stairs and ramps (ARC-STAIR-002, ARC-RAMP-001).

    Behaviour & rules. - Per segment (Edit Path): Height Correction = By Type or a custom value; Slope = By Host, Flat or Sloped. - Type parameters: - Railing Height: the height of the top-most rail; - Rail Structure (Non-Continuous): rows of Name, Height, Offset, Profile and Material; - Baluster Placement (ARC-RAIL-002); - Baluster Offset; - Use Landing Height Adjustment and the amount; - Angled Joins: Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments or Add No Connector; - Tangent Joins: Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments, No Connector or Extend Rails to Meet; - Rail Connections: Trim or Weld; - Top Rail: height and type; - Handrail 1 and Handrail 2: type and Position (Left, Right, Left and Right, or None). - Instance parameters: Base Level, Base Offset, Offset from Path, Tread/Stringer Offset (on stairs), Length and phasing. - Path elevation for each segment: - By Host: the path follows the host surface. On stairs, the path height at a point on a run is the height of the nosing line under it. On landings it is the landing's top. When Use Landing Height Adjustment is on, the landing value is shifted by the adjustment. - Flat: constant at the segment's start height. - Sloped: linear between the segment's two end heights. - Transitions between a sloped and a flat segment follow the join rules: Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments inserts a vertical jog or a horizontal extension so that rails meet; No Connector leaves a gap; Extend Rails to Meet (tangent joins) extends the rails to their intersection. - Non-continuous rails. Each rail row is the path offset horizontally by the row's offset plus Offset from Path, lifted by the row's height above the path elevation. The rail profile is swept along the offset path with BRepOffsetAPI_MakePipeShell (auxiliary +Z binormal on flat segments; a Frenet frame is avoided so that the profile does not twist). At each segment join, rails are trimmed (Trim) or fused (Weld). - Continuous rails (Top Rail, Handrail 1 and Handrail 2) are sub-elements, selectable with Tab. - Type parameters: Construction (Default Join: Fillet or Miter; Fillet Radius; Hand Clearance; Profile; Projection; Transitions: Gooseneck, None or Simple); Extensions at the beginning (bottom) and end (top) (Style: Wall, Floor or Post; Length; Plus Tread Depth); Terminations; Supports (family; Layout: Fixed Distance, Align with Posts, Fixed Number, Maximum Spacing or Minimum Spacing; Spacing; Justification). - Editing: Edit Rail (edits the path for extensions) and Edit Rail Joins (per join: By Type, Fillet, Miter or Flush). - Generation: the continuous path is built and then filleted at joins with the fillet radius (Geom2dAPI fillet in plan, then lifted). Extensions are appended, the profile is swept, and support families are placed along the path by the support layout. The layout uses the same algorithm as the curtain grid solver (ARC-CW-003) applied to path length.

    Data (IFC mapping). - IfcRailing (PredefinedType = GUARDRAIL, or HANDRAIL when the type has no balusters, or BALUSTRADE when balusters are densely spaced; the user can override this) with an IfcRailingType. It aggregates: - continuous rails as nested IfcRailing(HANDRAIL) (4X3: IfcRail is not used, because it belongs to railway rails); - non-continuous rails as IfcMember (USERDEFINED, ObjectType "RAIL"); - balusters as IfcMember (USERDEFINED, ObjectType "BALUSTER"); - posts as IfcMember(POST); - supports as IfcMember (USERDEFINED, ObjectType "RAILSUPPORT"). - The railing is related to its host through IfcRelConnectsElements (Name "HostedBy") and, for stairs, through aggregation into the IfcStair. - Pset_RailingCommon holds Height, IsExternal and Diameter (for round handrails). - The path is stored in RXD element data (sketch), and the rail and baluster tables in RXD type data (recipe.railing_type).

    Commands. - railing.create(type_id, path: [curve], host_ref?, base_level?, base_offset?, offset_from_path?, segment_slopes?: [ByHost|Flat|Sloped], height_corrections?: [f64|ByType]) -> element_id - railing.place_on_host(type_id, host_id, position: Treads|Stringer) -> [element_id] - railing.edit_path(railing_id, path, ...) - railing.flip_path(railing_id) - railing.set_rail_join(railing_id, join_ref, mode: ByType|Fillet|Miter|Flush) - railingtype.set_rails(type_id, rows) - railingtype.set_continuous_rail(type_id, which: Top|Handrail1|Handrail2, props)

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A railing on a straight stair run with By Host follows the nosing line at a constant vertical height. On the landing it is flat, and the join is made with a vertical segment when Angled Joins = Add Vertical/Horizontal Segments. - [ ] A top rail with Fillet joins of radius 50 mm has continuous tangents at every corner. - [ ] A handrail with Position = Left and Right on a two-run stair produces two handrails, with wall extensions of the configured length at the bottom and the top.

    3.7.8 Baluster placement

    ID: ARC-RAIL-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §8.5 (Edit Baluster Placement), §17.9

    Purpose. A deterministic algorithm for placing balusters and posts.

    Behaviour & rules. - Main pattern rows. Each row has: Name, Baluster Family (or None), Base (Host, Top of Rail Structure or a rail name), Base Offset, Top (Top Rail Elevation or a rail name), Top Offset, Distance from previous, and Offset (perpendicular to the path). - Pattern settings: - Pattern Length P = the sum of all Distance from previous values, plus the distance from the last row to the end of the pattern; - Break Pattern at: Each Segment End, Angles Greater Than α, or Never; - Justify: Beginning, End, Center or Spread Pattern to Fit; - Excess length fill: None, Truncate, Repeat Pattern, or Spacing (with a baluster family and spacing value). - Posts: Start, Corner and End post rows (family, base, top and their offsets, Space and Offset). Corner Posts At: Each Segment End, Angles Greater Than or Never. - Stairs: Use Baluster Per Tread On Stairs, Balusters Per Tread b and its family. On stair runs this overrides the main pattern. - Algorithm. 1. Split the path into pattern runs at break points: segment ends, or joins whose deflection angle is greater than α, according to Break Pattern at. Every length s is measured along the path in plan. 2. Place posts. A start post goes at s = 0 of the path. An end post goes at s = L (open paths only). A corner post goes at each break point that meets the Corner Posts At rule. Each post at position s_p reserves [s_p − Space, s_p + Space]. 3. For each pattern run of length Λ (between s_a and s_b): - Beginning: the pattern origin is s_a. Instances are placed at s_a + kP + d_i while < s_b. - End: the same, mirrored from s_b. - Center: the origin is s_a + (Λ − ⌊Λ/P⌋·P)/2. - Spread Pattern to Fit: m = max(1, round(Λ/P)), P' = Λ/m, and every distance in the pattern is scaled by P'/P. Excess fill does not apply. - Excess length fill (for the leftover r = Λ − ⌊Λ/P⌋·P): None leaves r empty. Truncate places pattern rows from the start of the pattern while they fit within r. Repeat Pattern places one more full pattern starting in r and keeps the rows that fall before s_b. Spacing fills r with the excess-fill family at the given spacing, using Center justification within r. 4. Remove every baluster that falls inside a post's reserved interval. 5. Per-tread override on stair runs (when enabled): for each tread i, with its nosing at s_i and depth T, place b balusters at s_i + T·(j − ½)/b for j = 1…b, measured from the nosing toward the next riser. Then apply the baluster offset. 6. Heights. Each baluster runs from its Base reference (the host surface height at s, from the path elevation; or the height of the named rail) plus the base offset, up to its Top reference plus the top offset. The family is stretched to that length. Where the top reference is sloped, the family's top is cut by the plane of the rail's underside (BRepAlgoAPI_Cut). 7. Balusters are instances of their family, written as mapped items in IFC.

    Commands. railingtype.set_baluster_pattern(type_id, rows, break_at, angle?, justify, excess_fill, excess_family?, excess_spacing?), railingtype.set_posts(type_id, start, corner, end, corner_at, angle?) and railingtype.set_per_tread(type_id, enabled, count, family_id).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A 3.05 m straight path with a one-row pattern (Distance from previous = 0.12 m, so P = 0.12 m), Beginning justification, Excess fill = None, and start and end posts with Space 0.05 m: the candidate positions are 0.12, 0.24 … 3.00 (25 positions). The one at 3.00 lies inside the end post's reserved interval [3.00, 3.10] and is removed, leaving 24 balusters. - [ ] Spread Pattern to Fit on a 3.05 m path with P = 0.12 gives 25 patterns of 0.122 m. - [ ] With 2 balusters per tread on 0.28 m treads, balusters sit 0.07 m and 0.21 m behind each nosing.

    3.7.9 Ramps

    ID: ARC-RAMP-001 · Priority: P1 · Ref: research/02 §8.6

    Workflow. 1. The user starts Architecture › Circulation › Ramp in a plan or 3D view. 2. In the sketch (Modify | Create Ramp Sketch), the user either uses Run (Line or Center-ends Arc), which is the simplest option and adds landings automatically when a run exceeds Maximum Incline Length, or draws Boundary and Riser curves for custom shapes. 3. Tools › Railing chooses the railing type. 4. Finish.

    Behaviour & rules. - Instance parameters: Base Level, Base Offset, Top Level, Top Offset, Multistory Top Level, Text (Up/Down), Width. - Type parameters: Thickness (used when Shape = Thick), Function, Text Size and Font, Ramp Material, Maximum Incline Length, Ramp Max Slope (1/x), Shape (Thick or Solid) and identity data. - Length. The required horizontal length is H · x, where H is the height and 1/x the maximum slope. When the run tool is used, the tooltip shows the remaining length. A drawn run that is too short raises "Ramp slope exceeds maximum", and the ramp is still created. - Automatic landings. When a straight run's length exceeds Maximum Incline Length, Reviera inserts a landing whose depth equals the ramp width. Runs between landings share the height in proportion to their lengths. - Geometry. - Thick: the top surface is a ruled surface between the boundary curves, rising linearly along the run path. The ramp is a slab of the given thickness under it, built as BRepOffsetAPI_ThruSections of cross-sections every 0.5 m along curved paths, or a prism for straight runs. - Solid: the volume between the top surface and the base level. - Usability tip carried into the UI: when the default top level would make the ramp unrealistically long, Reviera suggests setting the top level to the base level with a small top offset. - Sloped or shape-edited floors are an accepted alternative way to model ramps.

    Data (IFC mapping). IfcRamp (STRAIGHT_RUN_RAMP, TWO_STRAIGHT_RUN_RAMP, QUARTER_TURN_RAMP, TWO_QUARTER_TURN_RAMP, HALF_TURN_RAMP or SPIRAL_RAMP, classified as for stairs) with an IfcRampType, aggregating IfcRampFlight (STRAIGHT or SPIRAL), IfcSlab(LANDING) and IfcRailing. Pset_RampCommon holds RequiredSlope and IsExternal, and Pset_RampFlightCommon holds Headroom, ClearWidth and Slope. The sketch is stored in RXD element data (sketch).

    Commands. ramp.create(type_id, base_level, top_level | Unconnected(h), base_offset?, top_offset?, runs?: [curve], boundary?: [[curve],[curve]], risers?: [curve], width?, railing?) -> element_id and ramp.edit_sketch(ramp_id, ...).

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A ramp 0.6 m high at 1:12 with Maximum Incline Length 6 m, drawn as one straight run, is 7.2 m long and gets one landing between two 3.6 m runs.

    3.8 Openings

    3.8.1 Opening by face

    ID: ARC-OPEN-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §9

    Workflow. The user starts Architecture › Opening › By Face, picks a face of a floor, roof, ceiling, beam, brace or column, sketches a closed shape on it, and presses Finish.

    Behaviour & rules. The sketch plane is the picked face's plane. The opening solid is the sketch region extruded along the face normal, through the host's full thickness plus 1 mm on each side. It is subtracted from the host (BRepAlgoAPI_Cut). On a curved face, the sketch is projected onto the face's tangent plane at the pick point. The opening can be edited with Edit Sketch.

    Data (IFC mapping). IfcOpeningElement (OPENING) related to the host through IfcRelVoidsElement, with a body of IfcExtrudedAreaSolid along the face normal. The sketch is stored in RXD element data (sketch).

    Commands. opening.create_by_face(host_ref, loops) -> element_id.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] An opening by face on a 30° roof cuts at right angles to the roof surface, so its sides lean 30° from vertical.

    3.8.2 Vertical opening

    ID: ARC-OPEN-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §9

    Purpose. A plan-shaped hole through one slab-like element, with vertical sides whatever the slope of the element.

    Workflow. 1. The user starts Architecture › Opening › Vertical in a plan, ceiling plan, section, elevation or 3D view and picks a floor (architectural or structural), roof or ceiling. 2. Sketch mode opens on the host's level (in a section or elevation, the user picks a plan view through Go To View). The user sketches one or more closed loops with the draw tools or Pick Lines. 3. Finish Edit Mode creates the opening. Selecting it later offers Edit Sketch.

    Behaviour & rules. The user picks a floor, roof or ceiling, sketches loops in plan and presses Finish. The opening is extruded vertically through the whole host, whatever the host's slope, and it cuts that host only. - Sketch rules. Loops must be closed and must not intersect each other (ARC-SKCH-002). Several loops make one opening element with several voids. A loop that lies partly outside the host is allowed: the part outside cuts nothing, and the host's edge is notched. A loop entirely outside the host is an error on Finish ("Opening does not intersect host"). - Extent. The void runs from below the host's lowest point to above its highest point (host bounding box plus 1 mm each way), so it cuts sloped, shape-edited and warped hosts completely. - Following the host. The opening is hosted: it moves with the host, is copied with it and is deleted with it. If the host's boundary is edited so that the opening no longer intersects it, the opening stays and reports "Opening does not intersect host". - Other elements. Only the picked host is cut. To cut several elements on several levels, use a shaft (ARC-OPEN-004). Rooms are not affected, but an opening in a room-bounding floor or ceiling is subtracted when room volumes are computed (ARC-ROOM-002), because the cut host is used. - Instance parameters: Phase Created and Phase Demolished only; a vertical opening has no height parameters. - Hosting. Elements hosted on the cut face (for example, face-based fixtures) inside the opening lose their host and are reported as orphaned (ARC-HOST-001).

    Data (IFC mapping). An IfcOpeningElement whose body is an IfcExtrudedAreaSolid with Z direction, related to the host through IfcRelVoidsElement. PredefinedType = OPENING. The loops are stored in RXD element data (sketch) on the opening.

    Commands. opening.create_vertical(host_id, loops) -> element_id; sketch.begin(opening_id) edits the loops afterwards.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A vertical opening in a 30° roof has vertical sides. - [ ] A 1 × 1 m loop that half overlaps the edge of a floor notches the floor by 0.5 m² and nothing else. - [ ] A vertical opening in the upper of two stacked floors leaves the lower floor intact. - [ ] Moving the host floor 2 m moves the opening with it.

    3.8.3 Wall opening

    ID: ARC-OPEN-003 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §4.11, §9

    Workflow. The user starts Opening › Wall in an elevation, section or 3D view, picks a straight or arc wall, and drags a rectangle.

    Behaviour & rules. - The opening is a rectangle in the wall's developed (u, z) plane. Afterward, drag controls and temporary dimensions edit it, and it can be moved along the wall. - Instance parameters: Base Constraint, Base Offset, Top Constraint, Top Offset and Unconnected Height. - The cut goes through the wall's full thickness, normal to the location curve. On curved slanted walls the cut is therefore not rectangular in plan. - The opening produces mid-end faces (ARC-JOIN-001). - Cased openings use a loadable passage-opening family, which is an insert.

    Data (IFC mapping). An IfcOpeningElement related to the wall through IfcRelVoidsElement, with no filling element.

    Commands. opening.create_wall(wall_id, u0, u1, base: {level_id, offset}, top: Level{id,offset} | Unconnected(h)) -> element_id.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A wall opening that follows its base and top levels grows when the top level is raised.

    3.8.4 Shaft opening

    ID: ARC-OPEN-004 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §9

    Workflow. The user starts Opening › Shaft in a plan view, sketches the boundary (lines, or Pick Walls) and optional Symbolic Lines (shown at every cut level), and presses Finish.

    Behaviour & rules. - Instance parameters: Base Constraint (defaults to the active plan level), Base Offset, Top Constraint, Top Offset and Unconnected Height. - The shaft solid is the boundary region extruded from z_base to z_top. It cuts every floor, roof, ceiling and toposolid that it intersects. Walls, structural framing and families are not cut. - When the shaft is moved in any view, it moves everywhere. - Implementation. The shaft queries the R-tree for cuttable elements that overlap its bounding box. It adds a cut edge to each one and keeps that list up to date as elements are added, moved or deleted. Each host gets its own derived opening.

    Data (IFC mapping). The shaft itself is an IfcBuildingElementProxy with PredefinedType = PROVISIONFORVOID and the full prism as its body. For each host it cuts, Reviera writes a separate IfcOpeningElement (the part of the prism within the host, plus 1 mm), related to the host through IfcRelVoidsElement. Each derived opening records the shaft it comes from in RXD element data (recipe.opening). The symbolic lines are annotation (DOC chapter).

    Commands. opening.create_shaft(loops, base_level, base_offset?, top: Level{id,offset} | Unconnected(h), symbolic_lines?: [curve]) -> element_id.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A shaft from Level 1 to Roof cuts every floor between them. A floor added later in that range is cut automatically. - [ ] The IFC export contains one IfcOpeningElement per cut host, and each one is voided correctly.

    3.8.5 Dormer opening

    ID: ARC-OPEN-005 · Priority: P1 · Ref: research/02 §9

    Workflow. 1. The user models the dormer walls and the dormer roof, and joins the dormer roof to the main roof with Join/Unjoin Roof (ARC-ROOF-006). 2. The user starts Opening › Dormer and picks the main roof. 3. With Pick Roof/Wall Edges, the user picks the boundary. Valid references are: the joined roof or its bottom face, the side faces of walls, the bottom faces of floors, the edges of the roof being cut, and model lines on its face. 4. Finish.

    Behaviour & rules. - The picked references form a closed loop, projected onto the main roof's top surface. The opening solid is that loop extruded vertically down through the main roof, but limited to the region below the dormer roof's underside and inside the dormer walls' interior faces. As a result, the cut is vertical at the dormer walls and horizontal (following the dormer roof) at the top. - The loop stays locked to the picked references.

    Data (IFC mapping). An IfcOpeningElement in each affected IfcSlab of the main roof.

    Commands. opening.create_dormer(roof_id, refs: [ref]) -> element_id.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A dormer opening moves with the dormer walls when they are moved 300 mm along the roof.

    3.9 Rooms, areas and colour schemes

    3.9.1 Rooms

    ID: ARC-ROOM-001 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §10.1

    Purpose. Spaces bounded by room-bounding elements, which carry identity, finishes and computed quantities.

    Workflow. 1. The user starts Architecture › Room & Area › Room (RM) in a plan view. 2. The user sets the options on the contextual tab: - Tag on Placement (on by default); - Upper Limit (a level) and Offset (default 4000 mm, or 10' in imperial templates); - tag orientation (Horizontal, Vertical or Model) and Leader; - Room: New or an existing unplaced room. 3. A click inside an enclosed region places the room. Place Rooms Automatically places a room in every enclosed region larger than 0.25 sq ft (0.023 m²) on the level, numbered in sequence. 4. Highlight Boundaries shows all room-bounding elements in a highlight colour and opens a warning list.

    UI. The Room & Area panel holds: Room, Room Separator, Tag Room (RT), Tag All Not Tagged, Area and Volume Computations, Area, Area Boundary, Tag Area, and Color Schemes.

    Behaviour & rules. - Room-bounding elements by default: walls (basic, curtain, in-place and face-based), roofs, floors, ceilings (including in-place and face-based ones), architectural columns, structural columns whose material is concrete, curtain systems, and room separation lines. Every one of these has a Room Bounding parameter. Linked models bound rooms when their link type has Room Bounding on (COL chapter). - Narrow regions. If the region has no point at least 153 mm (half of 306 mm) from its boundary — that is, if the region is too narrow (computed by an inward polygon offset) — placement is rejected with "Room is too narrow". - Not enclosed. Placing a room in an unenclosed region creates the room with Area = Not Enclosed and the warning "Room is not in a properly enclosed region". - Redundant rooms. A second room in a region that already has a room is Redundant ("Multiple rooms are in the same enclosed region"). Both rooms take the region's area, and both are flagged. - Room Separator. These lines (Line, Arc and Pick Lines) split space. Rooms update automatically. They are visible in plan and 3D, and are controlled by the "Room Separation" line subcategory. - Tags snap to the room reference point, which is the intersection of the room's two reference lines. Initially these lines run through the centroid of the boundary's bounding box. Re-center Reference Lines (Modify | Rooms) recomputes them, and Move to Room Reference (Modify | Room Tags) moves tags back to that point. - Unplaced rooms. Deleting a room in a view unplaces it: it stays in the project, schedules list it as Not Placed, and it can be placed again from the Room tool's Room list. Deleting it from a room schedule removes it permanently. - Phases. Rooms belong to one phase. They can be copied between phases, and boundaries are computed with the elements that exist in that phase. - Instance parameters: Level (RO), Upper Limit, Limit Offset, Base Offset, Area, Perimeter, Unbounded Height, Volume (when enabled), Computation Height (RO, from the level), Number, Name, Comments, Occupancy, Department, Base Finish, Ceiling Finish, Wall Finish, Floor Finish, Occupant and Phase.

    Data (IFC mapping). - IfcSpace (PredefinedType = INTERNAL; EXTERNAL for rooms flagged as exterior) aggregated (IfcRelAggregates) under its IfcBuildingStorey. Name = Number and LongName = Name, which is the usual IFC convention. - Representations. FootPrint (IfcGeometricCurveSet / IfcArbitraryProfileDefWithVoids curves) and Body (an IfcExtrudedAreaSolid from base to upper limit, or the clipped room solid as an IfcFacetedBrep when volume computation is on and the room is clipped). - Quantities and properties. Qto_SpaceBaseQuantities: NetFloorArea, GrossFloorArea, NetPerimeter, GrossPerimeter, Height, NetVolume and FinishCeilingHeight. Pset_SpaceCommon: Reference, IsExternal and the finish properties where Pset_SpaceCoveringRequirements applies (FloorCovering, WallCovering, CeilingCovering). - Space boundaries. Each boundary segment is written as an IfcRelSpaceBoundary (1st level: PhysicalOrVirtualBoundary = PHYSICAL for elements, VIRTUAL for separation lines; InternalOrExternalBoundary from the wall's function), with ConnectionGeometry (an IfcConnectionCurveGeometry at the computation height). - Room separation lines are IfcVirtualElement (4X3: PredefinedType = BOUNDARY) with an Axis representation. - Unplaced rooms are IfcSpace objects without a representation, still aggregated under the storey, and listed in RXD document model/rooms.

    Commands. - room.place(level_id, point, upper_limit?: level_id, limit_offset?, base_offset?, name?, number?, phase_id?, room_id?: existing_unplaced, tag?: {type_id, orientation, leader}) -> element_id - room.place_automatically(level_id, phase_id?) -> [element_id] - room.unplace(room_ids) - room.delete(room_ids) - roomseparator.create(level_id, curves: [curve]) -> [element_id] - room.recenter_reference(room_ids) - roomtag.move_to_reference(tag_ids) - room.highlight_boundaries(view_id) -> [element_id] (query)

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] Place Rooms Automatically on a level with six enclosed regions creates six rooms numbered 1–6, and none for a 0.01 m² gap. - [ ] Deleting a placed room in plan makes it Not Placed in the room schedule. Placing it again keeps its Number and Name. - [ ] Every room exports as IfcSpace with Name = Number and LongName = Name, and with at least one IfcRelSpaceBoundary per bounding wall.

    3.9.2 Room boundary computation

    ID: ARC-ROOM-002 · Priority: P0 · Ref: research/02 §10.1 (Room computation, Area and Volume Computations), §17.10 · web: Room Area and Volume

    Purpose. A deterministic, robust algorithm that computes room boundaries, areas, perimeters and volumes.

    Behaviour & rules.

    Settings (Area and Volume Computations, stored in RXD document model/rooms): - Volume Computations: Areas only (default) or Areas and Volumes. - Room Area Computation: At wall finish (default), At wall center, At wall core layer or At wall core center. - Area Schemes tab (ARC-AREA-001).

    These settings apply to the whole project. Walls that came from a non-parametric import (no RXD recipe) always use their actual faces, which is the finish rule.

    Area and Volume Computations dialog (Architecture › Room & Area panel drop-down): - Computations tab. Volume Computations is a pair of radio buttons (Areas only, Areas and Volumes) with a note that volume computation adds time to every room regeneration. Room Area Computation has four radio buttons for the area rules above and a small plan diagram of a wall showing where the boundary line falls for the selected rule. A read-only line shows the current computation height of the active view's level and a link that selects that level so its Computation Height can be edited (a level parameter, default 0; ARC-LVL-001). - Area Schemes tab. The list of area schemes with Name and Description, and New, Rename and Delete (ARC-AREA-001). Deleting a scheme that has area plans lists the plans that will be deleted and asks for confirmation. Names must be unique and non-empty. - Validation and effect. OK applies both tabs as one transaction. Changing the area rule or switching volumes on marks every room dirty, and the rooms are recomputed (in parallel by level) before the dialog closes; a progress bar appears when this takes longer than 0.5 s. Switching volumes off clears the stored volumes and makes Volume show "Not Computed". Cancel changes nothing.

    Commands. - room.computation_settings() -> () opens the dialog (UI only). - room.set_computation_settings(volumes?: AreasOnly|AreasAndVolumes, area_rule?: Finish|Center|Core|CoreCenter) -> () applies the settings without the dialog and triggers the recomputation. - The area-scheme commands are in ARC-AREA-001.

    Algorithm. Run per room. Rooms that share a level band and phase share the arrangement built in steps 2–3. 1. Computation plane. z_c = elev(Level) + Level.ComputationHeight. The computation height is a level parameter that defaults to 0. When the room's base offset puts the room's floor above z_c, Reviera uses z_c' = max(z_c, z_base + 1 mm). 2. Candidate collection. Query the bounding-box R-tree for elements whose 3D bounding box crosses z_c and the level's plan extent, then keep those that meet all of these: - RoomBounding = true (from the host model, or from linked models whose link is room-bounding); - they exist in the room's phase (created in or before that phase and not demolished in or before it); - they are not inside an excluded design option (the room sees the primary option, plus the option it belongs to); - they are one of: - vertical bounding elements (walls, columns, curtain walls and systems, in-place and face-based elements in bounding categories); - room separation lines on the room's level (whatever their height). 3. Sectioning. For each candidate, compute its plan trace at z_c. - Walls, according to the area rule: - finish: section the wall's uncut body — the body after joins and attachment, but before insert voids, wall openings and reveals are cut — with the plane z = z_c (BRepAlgoAPI_Section with gp_Pln), and take the closed loops (ShapeAnalysis_FreeBounds::ConnectEdgesToWires). Using the uncut body stops doors and windows from connecting rooms. Wall sweeps take part only if their own Room Bounding is on. - center: the wall's centreline curve (the geometric centre of the full thickness, not the location line). It is added as a zero-width boundary curve, trimmed to the join-resolved length. - core: section the core layers' union and take its loops. - core center: the core's centreline curve. - Profile-edited walls and attached walls are sectioned by their real geometry, so a notch that lies below z_c opens the boundary. - Columns, in-place elements and curtain systems: section loops. Curtain walls use the curve along the panel centre plane. - Room separation lines: their curves, as zero-width boundary curves. 4. Planar arrangement. Insert every loop edge and every zero-width curve into a 2D arrangement (a doubly-connected edge list). - Vertices within TOL_ROOM_SNAP are merged, and nearly collinear overlapping edges are merged. - Intersections are computed with a sweep-line over a uniform grid (exact line/line and line/arc intersections; other curves are flattened to a chord error of 0.1 mm), and edges are split at every intersection. - Each face of the arrangement is classified as solid when it lies inside a sectioned solid loop (a point-in-loop test on the original loop) or void otherwise. - Each half-edge records its source element (GlobalId), the sub-reference of the face it came from, and the rule that produced it. 5. Region. Locate the placement point p (or the room reference point for existing rooms) in the arrangement. - If p lies in a solid face, report "Room placement point is inside an element" and do not move the room. Placing interactively at such a point is rejected. - If p lies in the unbounded face, the room is Not Enclosed. - Otherwise, the room region Ω is the void face that contains p. Its boundary consists of an outer loop and zero or more inner loops (islands such as free-standing columns). 6. Clean-up. - Antennas (dangling edges: degree-1 chains inside Ω, such as a separation line that stops in the middle of the room) remain boundary segments for reference but contribute nothing to area or perimeter. - Free-standing walls inside Ω create inner loops; their footprint is excluded from the area, and their faces count toward the perimeter. - Too narrow: Ω is offset inward by 153 mm (BRepOffsetAPI_MakeOffset on the face, or a robust 2D offset). If the result is empty, the room is "Too narrow". For an existing room this keeps the area but flags it. 7. Area and perimeter. - Area = |∫ over Ω|, computed exactly for line and arc edges with the shoelace formula plus circular-segment terms, and to 1e-9 relative accuracy for other curves. - Perimeter = the sum of the lengths of the outer and inner loops, excluding antennas. 8. Redundant rooms. If two placed rooms of the same phase locate to the same Ω, both report the area of Ω. The one placed later is flagged Redundant. 9. Volume (when Areas and Volumes is on): - The band is z_b = elev(Level) + BaseOffset to z_t = elev(UpperLimit) + LimitOffset. Unbounded Height is z_t − z_b. - Seed prism Q = Prism(Ω ⊕ m, z_b, z_t), where ⊕ m is an outward offset by m. The margin m is the largest horizontal distance by which any bounding vertical element in the band deviates from its trace at z_c (for example, slanted walls). It is computed from the element bounding boxes, and is 0 when all elements are vertical. - Subtract every room-bounding solid that crosses Q: vertical elements (uncut bodies, as in step 3) and horizontal elements (floors, ceilings, roofs and their in-place equivalents). Use BRepAlgoAPI_Cut with all tools in one operation (SetTools), SetRunParallel(true) and the fuzzy value. - The room solid is the connected component (TopExp over solids) that contains the point (p, z_c). If ceilings or roofs do not close the top, the solid simply reaches z_t. - Volume = GProp volume of that solid. 10. Outputs. - The boundary segments are an ordered list of (curve, source element GlobalId or separation line, sub-reference) for each loop. Wall finish computation, tag placement, "By Room" wall creation (ARC-WALL-014), door From/To (ARC-DOOR-001) and IfcRelSpaceBoundary export all use this list. - The room's FootPrint is Ω. 11. Incremental regeneration. - A room depends (bound edges) on every element returned by the candidate query in step 2, and on the level, the upper limit level and the phase. - When any of those elements changes geometry, Room Bounding, phase or design option, the room is marked dirty. So is any room whose band contains the changed element's new or old bounding box. - Dirty rooms that share a level and phase are recomputed together, with one arrangement per (level, phase, computation height). Different levels run in parallel.

    Acceptance criteria. - [ ] A 5 m × 4 m room (finish to finish) bounded by 200 mm walls reports 20.000 m² At wall finish, 21.840 m² At wall center, and an 18.000 m perimeter at the finish faces. - [ ] room.set_computation_settings(area_rule: Center) updates every room's area in one undo step; undoing it restores the finish-face areas.
